cards.front: How do ribose and deoxyribose differ?
cards.back: Deoxyribose lacks the OH on carbon 2, so it has one fewer hydroxyl. DNA uses deoxyribose and RNA uses ribose.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Extras/Molecules of Life/02 Carbohydrates

cards.front: What is allolactose and how is IPTG used?
cards.back: Allolactose is the natural inducer of the lac operon. IPTG mimics it but can't be broken down, so it keeps the operon on in the lab.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Extras/Molecules of Life/02 Carbohydrates

cards.front: Which functional groups are in serine?
cards.back: Amino, carboxyl and a hydroxyl in the R group.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Extras/Molecules of Life/03 Amino acids

cards.front: How do amino acids exist at pH 7?
cards.back: As zwitterions: the amino group is NH₃⁺ and the carboxyl is COO⁻.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Extras/Molecules of Life/03 Amino acids

cards.front: What does the cis double bond in oleic acid do?
cards.back: It puts a kink in the chain, so the chains pack less tightly and the fat stays liquid.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Extras/Molecules of Life/04 Lipids

cards.front: How do ATP and cAMP differ?
cards.back: ATP has three phosphates in a chain on carbon 5 of ribose. In cAMP a single phosphate bridges carbons 3 and 5, making a ring.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Extras/Molecules of Life/05 Nucleotides and energy carriers

cards.front: Why is TRIS useful, and roughly what pH does it buffer?
cards.back: Its amino group gains and loses H⁺, so it resists pH change. It buffers around pH 8.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Extras/Molecules of Life/07 Buffers and lab reagents

cards.front: Which neurotransmitters are made from amino acids?
cards.back: Serotonin from tryptophan, dopamine and adrenaline from tyrosine, histamine from histidine, GABA from glutamate.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Extras/Molecules of Life/08 Signalling molecules

cards.front: Write the electron configurations of carbon and sodium.
cards.back: Carbon (6): 1s² 2s² 2p². Sodium (11): 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s¹.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/02 How Atoms Form Molecules/02 Recap, electron configurations

cards.front: What is the difference between two isotopes of an element?
cards.back: The same number of protons but a different number of neutrons.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/02 How Atoms Form Molecules/02 Recap, electron configurations

cards.front: Why do atoms form bonds?
cards.back: To reach the most stable state, a full outer (valence) shell. Noble gases already have one, so they are unreactive.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/02 How Atoms Form Molecules/03 Why atoms form molecules

cards.front: Why is chromium [Ar] 4s¹ 3d⁵ rather than 4s² 3d⁴?
cards.back: Half-filled orbitals are extra stable and 4s and 3d are almost equal in energy, so one 4s electron moves to 3d.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/02 How Atoms Form Molecules/04 Electron configuration exceptions

cards.front: Is the bond in O₂ single, double or triple? And in F₂?
cards.back: O₂: double (two shared pairs). F₂: single.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/02 How Atoms Form Molecules/06 Covalent bonding

cards.front: What is a dative bond? Give an example.
cards.back: A covalent bond where both electrons come from one atom's lone pair, e.g. N–H in NH₄⁺ formed when NH₃ bonds to H⁺.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/02 How Atoms Form Molecules/07 Dative (coordinate) bonds

cards.front: How does an ionic bond differ from a covalent bond?
cards.back: Ionic: electrons are transferred, forming cations and anions held by electrostatic attraction. Covalent: a pair of electrons is shared between two atoms.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/02 How Atoms Form Molecules/08 Ionic or covalent

cards.front: Is KCl ionic or covalent, and why?
cards.back: Ionic: K easily loses an electron and Cl easily gains one, so K⁺ and Cl⁻ form.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/02 How Atoms Form Molecules/08 Ionic or covalent

cards.front: What is electronegativity and what affects it?
cards.back: An atom's ability to pull electrons in a covalent bond towards itself. It depends on the number of protons and the distance of the outer electrons from the nucleus.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/02 How Atoms Form Molecules/09 Electronegativity

cards.front: What happens when atoms with very different electronegativities bond?
cards.back: A very large difference gives an ionic bond. A smaller but significant difference gives a polar covalent bond with δ+ and δ− ends.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/03 Molecular Structure/01 Polar bonds

cards.front: Why is water polar, and what does that allow?
cards.back: O is much more electronegative than H, so O is δ− and the H atoms δ+. Water molecules attract each other through hydrogen bonds.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/03 Molecular Structure/02 Polar molecules and water

cards.front: How can carbon make four identical bonds if its 2s and 2p electrons differ?
cards.back: Hybridisation: the 2s and three 2p orbitals mix into four identical sp³ orbitals pointing to the corners of a tetrahedron.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/03 Molecular Structure/03 Carbon and its electrons

cards.front: What are sp, sp² and sp³ hybridisation, with angles?
cards.back: sp: 2 hybrids, 180°. sp²: 3 hybrids, 120°. sp³: 4 hybrids, 109.5°.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/03 Molecular Structure/04 Hybridisation

cards.front: What is the difference between a σ and a π bond?
cards.back: σ: head-on overlap, present in every bond. π: side-on overlap of unhybridised p orbitals, adding the second and third bonds of a double or triple bond.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/03 Molecular Structure/05 Sigma and pi bonds

cards.front: State the VSEPR repulsion order.
cards.back: Lone pair–lone pair > lone pair–bond > bond–bond.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/03 Molecular Structure/06 Shapes of molecules, VSEPR

cards.front: What shape is chloroform, CHCl₃?
cards.back: Tetrahedral: C has 4 bonds and no lone pairs.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/03 Molecular Structure/07 Worked shapes

cards.front: What shape is ammonia, and why isn't it tetrahedral?
cards.back: Trigonal pyramidal: 4 electron regions arranged tetrahedrally, but one is a lone pair, so only 3 positions hold atoms.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/03 Molecular Structure/07 Worked shapes

cards.front: What shapes are CH₂O and HCN?
cards.back: CH₂O: trigonal planar (C=O double bond, sp²). HCN: linear (C≡N triple bond, sp).
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/03 Molecular Structure/07 Worked shapes

cards.front: What does 'R' mean in R–OH?
cards.back: The rest of the molecule: any carbon chain carrying the group.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/04 Functional Groups in Biology/01 Organic compounds and R groups

cards.front: What makes an alkane saturated?
cards.back: Only single bonds, so every carbon has its maximum number of bonded hydrogens.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/04 Functional Groups in Biology/02 Alkanes

cards.front: What is an alkyl group?
cards.back: An alkane with one hydrogen removed so it can attach to another molecule, e.g. methyl –CH₃.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/04 Functional Groups in Biology/03 Alkyl and aryl groups

cards.front: How does the slide's definition of an aryl group differ from most textbooks?
cards.back: The slide says a group from a cyclic alkane. Textbooks mean an aromatic ring such as phenyl; a ring alkane gives a cycloalkyl group.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/04 Functional Groups in Biology/03 Alkyl and aryl groups

cards.front: What is the difference between an alkane and an alkene?
cards.back: An alkene has a C=C double bond (two fewer H), so it is unsaturated.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/04 Functional Groups in Biology/04 Alkenes

cards.front: Name the groups: –OH, –COOH, C=O, –NH₂, –SH.
cards.back: Hydroxyl, carboxyl, carbonyl, amino, thiol.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/04 Functional Groups in Biology/05 Hydroxyl and carboxyl groups

cards.front: How do aldehydes and ketones differ?
cards.back: Both have a carbonyl group: at the end of the chain in an aldehyde, in the middle in a ketone.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/04 Functional Groups in Biology/06 Aldehydes and ketones

cards.front: Why do oxygen-containing groups make molecules polar?
cards.back: Oxygen is much more electronegative than C and H, so C–O and O–H bonds are polar. C–H bonds are not.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/04 Functional Groups in Biology/07 Oxygen makes molecules polar

cards.front: What bond joins two monosaccharides, and what is released?
cards.back: A glycosidic bond, formed by condensation, releasing water.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/04 Functional Groups in Biology/08 Carbohydrates and glycosidic bonds

cards.front: How does an ester form? Where are they found in biology?
cards.back: A carboxyl group reacts with a hydroxyl group, releasing water. Ester links join fatty acids to glycerol in fats.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/04 Functional Groups in Biology/09 Esters

cards.front: What are primary, secondary and tertiary amines?
cards.back: N bonded to 1, 2 or 3 carbons, e.g. methylamine, dimethylamine, trimethylamine.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/04 Functional Groups in Biology/10 Amino groups and amines

cards.front: How does a peptide bond form?
cards.back: The carboxyl group of one amino acid joins the amino group of the next, releasing water.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/04 Functional Groups in Biology/11 Peptide bonds

cards.front: What is a disulfide bridge and why does it matter?
cards.back: An S–S bond between two cysteine thiol groups that holds parts of a folded protein together.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/04 Functional Groups in Biology/12 Thiols and disulfide bridges

cards.front: What is the stoichiometry of N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃?
cards.back: 1 : 3 → 2. One N₂ reacts with three H₂ to give two NH₃.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/05 Chemical Reactions in Biology/01 Chemical reactions and stoichiometry

cards.front: Why can't H₂O be balanced by changing it to H₂O₂?
cards.back: Subscripts are part of the formula, so changing them makes a different substance. Only the coefficients in front change.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/05 Chemical Reactions in Biology/01 Chemical reactions and stoichiometry

cards.front: Balance C₆H₁₂O₆ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O.
cards.back: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O. Check: C 6 = 6, H 12 = 12, O 18 = 18.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/05 Chemical Reactions in Biology/02 Balancing equations, the oxidation of glucose

cards.front: Why do cells oxidise glucose in over 20 steps instead of one?
cards.back: Small steps let the energy be captured as chemical energy (ATP) instead of being lost all at once as heat.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/05 Chemical Reactions in Biology/02 Balancing equations, the oxidation of glucose

cards.front: What does a reaction mechanism show that a scheme does not?
cards.back: Which bonds break and form, the order they do it in, and how many steps the reaction takes.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/05 Chemical Reactions in Biology/03 Reaction scheme vs reaction mechanism

cards.front: What are the two ways valence electrons can redistribute in a reaction?
cards.back: As a pair moving together (heterolytic) or split, moving singly (homolytic).
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/05 Chemical Reactions in Biology/03 Reaction scheme vs reaction mechanism

cards.front: What does homolytic fission of Cl–Cl produce?
cards.back: Two chlorine free radicals, Cl•, each with one electron from the bond.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/05 Chemical Reactions in Biology/04 Homolytic and heterolytic bond breaking

cards.front: In heterolytic fission of H–Br, which atom keeps the electron pair and why?
cards.back: Bromine, because it is more electronegative. This gives H⁺ and Br⁻.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/05 Chemical Reactions in Biology/04 Homolytic and heterolytic bond breaking

cards.front: Name the three stages of a free radical reaction and what happens in each.
cards.back: Initiation: UV light splits a molecule into radicals. Propagation: a radical reacts to make a product and a new radical. Termination: two radicals combine into a stable molecule.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/05 Chemical Reactions in Biology/05 Free radical reactions

cards.front: Why does one chlorine radical lead to many chloromethane molecules?
cards.back: Each propagation step regenerates a radical (Cl• is remade in step 2), so the chain continues until termination.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/05 Chemical Reactions in Biology/05 Free radical reactions

cards.front: Which radicals from water and oxygen damage DNA?
cards.back: The hydroxyl radical (•OH) and superoxide (O₂•⁻).
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/05 Chemical Reactions in Biology/06 Free radicals and biological damage

cards.front: How do antioxidants such as vitamin C and E protect cells?
cards.back: They react with free radicals to form much less reactive radicals, stopping the chain of damage.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/05 Chemical Reactions in Biology/06 Free radicals and biological damage

cards.front: Define a nucleophile and give two examples.
cards.back: An electron-rich species with a lone pair it can donate to form a bond, such as OH⁻ and H₂O.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/05 Chemical Reactions in Biology/07 Nucleophiles and electrophiles

cards.front: What must every electrophile have?
cards.back: An empty valence orbital, so it can accept an electron pair.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/05 Chemical Reactions in Biology/07 Nucleophiles and electrophiles

cards.front: Why is the carbon in C–Br attacked by nucleophiles?
cards.back: Br is more electronegative, so it pulls the bond electrons towards itself, leaving carbon δ+ and electron-deficient.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/05 Chemical Reactions in Biology/08 Nucleophilic attack and polar bonds

cards.front: In nucleophilic attack, which way do the electrons move?
cards.back: From the nucleophile to the electrophile.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/05 Chemical Reactions in Biology/08 Nucleophilic attack and polar bonds

cards.front: What is the difference between addition and condensation?
cards.back: Addition keeps every atom of both reactants in one product. Condensation joins two molecules but also eliminates a small molecule, usually water.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/05 Chemical Reactions in Biology/09 The five reaction types

cards.front: Which reaction type breaks starch down into glucose?
cards.back: Hydrolysis.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/05 Chemical Reactions in Biology/09 The five reaction types

cards.front: In CH₃CH₂Br + OH⁻ → CH₃CH₂OH + Br⁻, identify the nucleophile, the electrophile and the leaving group.
cards.back: Nucleophile: OH⁻. Electrophile: the δ+ carbon bonded to Br. Leaving group: Br⁻.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/05 Chemical Reactions in Biology/10 Substitution

cards.front: In DNA synthesis, what is the nucleophile and what leaves?
cards.back: The 3′-OH at the end of the growing strand (or primer) is the nucleophile; pyrophosphate leaves.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/05 Chemical Reactions in Biology/10 Substitution

cards.front: Which two types of double bond take part in addition reactions?
cards.back: C=C in alkenes and C=O in carbonyl groups (aldehydes and ketones).
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/05 Chemical Reactions in Biology/11 Addition and hydration

cards.front: What forms when water adds to an aldehyde?
cards.back: A hydrate: a carbon carrying two –OH groups.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/05 Chemical Reactions in Biology/11 Addition and hydration

cards.front: What is eliminated when bromoethane forms ethene?
cards.back: H and Br from neighbouring carbons (overall HBr; with OH⁻ these leave as H₂O and Br⁻), leaving a C=C double bond.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/05 Chemical Reactions in Biology/12 Elimination

cards.front: How can OH⁻ cause both substitution and elimination with bromoethane?
cards.back: As a nucleophile it attacks the δ+ carbon (substitution). As a base it removes an H from the next carbon (elimination).
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/05 Chemical Reactions in Biology/12 Elimination

cards.front: Which reaction type makes proteins, DNA and polysaccharides, and what is released?
cards.back: Condensation, releasing water.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/05 Chemical Reactions in Biology/13 Condensation and hydrolysis

cards.front: Hydration vs hydrolysis: what is the difference?
cards.back: Both use water. Hydration adds it across a double bond, keeping one molecule. Hydrolysis uses it to break a bond, splitting the molecule in two.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/05 Chemical Reactions in Biology/13 Condensation and hydrolysis

cards.front: What is the difference between a transition state and an intermediate?
cards.back: A transition state is an energy maximum and cannot be isolated. An intermediate sits in an energy dip between two transition states, formed in one step and used up in the next.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/05 Chemical Reactions in Biology/14 Transition states and intermediates

cards.front: A reaction has three steps. How many transition states does it have, and which step sets the rate?
cards.back: Three. The step with the highest-energy transition state is the rate-limiting step.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/05 Chemical Reactions in Biology/14 Transition states and intermediates

cards.front: What is energy?
cards.back: The capacity to do work. Its SI unit is the joule (J).
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/06 Basic Principles of Physical Chemistry/01 Physical chemistry and energy in living things

cards.front: Why do cells need a constant supply of energy?
cards.back: They are highly ordered, and keeping that order requires constant work.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/06 Basic Principles of Physical Chemistry/01 Physical chemistry and energy in living things

cards.front: Name four forms of energy.
cards.back: Radiant (heat and light), mechanical, chemical and electrical.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/06 Basic Principles of Physical Chemistry/01 Physical chemistry and energy in living things

cards.front: What two ways can internal energy be transferred?
cards.back: As work (w) or as heat (q).
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/06 Basic Principles of Physical Chemistry/02 Internal energy, work and heat

cards.front: Write the equation linking internal energy, work and heat.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/06 Basic Principles of Physical Chemistry/02 Internal energy, work and heat

cards.front: State the first law of thermodynamics.
cards.back: The total energy of an isolated system is constant: energy cannot be created or destroyed, only converted from one form to another.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/06 Basic Principles of Physical Chemistry/03 The laws of thermodynamics

cards.front: State the second law of thermodynamics.
cards.back: Disorder (entropy) in the universe increases.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/06 Basic Principles of Physical Chemistry/03 The laws of thermodynamics

cards.front: Why must a living organism do work, according to the second law?
cards.back: To keep its internal order against the universal tendency towards disorder.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/06 Basic Principles of Physical Chemistry/03 The laws of thermodynamics

cards.front: Write the equation for kinetic energy and give the units.
cards.back: E = ½mv², with E in J, m in kg and v in m s⁻¹.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/06 Basic Principles of Physical Chemistry/04 Kinetic energy

cards.front: If an object's speed doubles, what happens to its kinetic energy?
cards.back: It quadruples, because E depends on v².
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/06 Basic Principles of Physical Chemistry/04 Kinetic energy

cards.front: Write the equation for gravitational potential energy.
cards.back: Ep = mgh, where g = 9.81 m s⁻².
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/06 Basic Principles of Physical Chemistry/05 Gravitational potential energy

cards.front: Trace the energy changes in a hydroelectric dam.
cards.back: Gravitational potential energy → kinetic energy of the flowing water → mechanical energy in the turbines → electrical energy.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/06 Basic Principles of Physical Chemistry/05 Gravitational potential energy

cards.front: Does breaking a bond release or require energy?
cards.back: It requires energy. Forming a bond releases energy.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/06 Basic Principles of Physical Chemistry/06 Chemical energy and bond energies

cards.front: Which needs more energy to break, a C–H bond or an N–H bond?
cards.back: C–H (412 kJ mol⁻¹) compared with N–H (390 kJ mol⁻¹).
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/06 Basic Principles of Physical Chemistry/06 Chemical energy and bond energies

cards.front: Why are bond energies in tables called average values?
cards.back: The energy of a bond depends on the other atoms attached, e.g. O–H in water differs from O–H in methanol.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/06 Basic Principles of Physical Chemistry/06 Chemical energy and bond energies

cards.front: Which is stronger, C=O or C–O, according to the table?
cards.back: C=O, 740 kJ mol⁻¹, compared with 358 kJ mol⁻¹ for C–O.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/06 Basic Principles of Physical Chemistry/06 Chemical energy and bond energies

cards.front: Define system and surroundings.
cards.back: The system is the part of interest inside a boundary; the surroundings are everything else in contact with it.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/06 Basic Principles of Physical Chemistry/07 System and surroundings

cards.front: What can an open system exchange with its surroundings that a closed system cannot?
cards.back: Matter. Both can exchange energy.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/06 Basic Principles of Physical Chemistry/07 System and surroundings

cards.front: Is a living cell an open, closed or isolated system?
cards.back: Open: it exchanges both matter and energy.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/06 Basic Principles of Physical Chemistry/07 System and surroundings

cards.front: Define heat in thermodynamics.
cards.back: The transfer of thermal energy from a region of higher temperature to one of lower temperature.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/06 Basic Principles of Physical Chemistry/08 Energy transfer as work and heat

cards.front: When a hot system cools, what happens to the total energy of system plus surroundings?
cards.back: It stays the same; thermal energy is just redistributed.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/06 Basic Principles of Physical Chemistry/08 Energy transfer as work and heat

cards.front: What energy conversion happens in a climber's muscles?
cards.back: Chemical energy (ATP) to kinetic energy, which raises the body and gives it gravitational potential energy.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/06 Basic Principles of Physical Chemistry/08 Energy transfer as work and heat

cards.front: What sign of ΔH means a reaction is exothermic?
cards.back: Negative: heat flows from the system to the surroundings.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/06 Basic Principles of Physical Chemistry/09 Enthalpy change, exothermic and endothermic

cards.front: Write the equation for ΔH from bond energies.
cards.back: ΔH = ΣE(reactants) − ΣE(products), the energy of bonds broken minus the energy of bonds formed.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/06 Basic Principles of Physical Chemistry/09 Enthalpy change, exothermic and endothermic

cards.front: Is the oxidation of glucose exothermic or endothermic?
cards.back: Exothermic: the products are lower in energy than the reactants.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/06 Basic Principles of Physical Chemistry/09 Enthalpy change, exothermic and endothermic

cards.front: What are the units of ΔH?
cards.back: J mol⁻¹ (often kJ mol⁻¹).
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/06 Basic Principles of Physical Chemistry/09 Enthalpy change, exothermic and endothermic

cards.front: State Hess's law.
cards.back: The total enthalpy change for a reaction is the same whichever route is taken from reactants to products.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/06 Basic Principles of Physical Chemistry/10 Hess's law and enthalpies of formation

cards.front: Write the equation for ΔH° from enthalpies of formation.
cards.back: ΔH°reaction = ΣΔHf°(products) − ΣΔHf°(reactants).
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/06 Basic Principles of Physical Chemistry/10 Hess's law and enthalpies of formation

cards.front: How does the order differ between the bond energy method and the enthalpy of formation method?
cards.back: Bond energies: reactants − products. Enthalpies of formation: products − reactants.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/06 Basic Principles of Physical Chemistry/10 Hess's law and enthalpies of formation

cards.front: What does a bomb calorimeter measure, and how?
cards.back: The enthalpy change of a reaction, as a temperature change of the surroundings inside an insulated chamber.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/06 Basic Principles of Physical Chemistry/11 Measuring enthalpy change by calorimetry

cards.front: If ΔH is negative, which are more stable, reactants or products?
cards.back: The products.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/06 Basic Principles of Physical Chemistry/11 Measuring enthalpy change by calorimetry

cards.front: Put solid, liquid and gas in order of increasing entropy.
cards.back: Solid < liquid < gas.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/06 Basic Principles of Physical Chemistry/12 Entropy

cards.front: Which has lower entropy, a folded or an unfolded protein?
cards.back: The folded protein, because it is more ordered.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/06 Basic Principles of Physical Chemistry/12 Entropy

cards.front: Why does proteolysis increase entropy?
cards.back: It increases the number of separate entities in the system.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/06 Basic Principles of Physical Chemistry/12 Entropy

cards.front: What are the units of entropy?
cards.back: J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/06 Basic Principles of Physical Chemistry/12 Entropy

cards.front: What must be true of ΔS(total) for a reaction to be spontaneous?
cards.back: It must be greater than zero.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/06 Basic Principles of Physical Chemistry/13 Entropy and spontaneous reactions

cards.front: How do highly ordered living things obey the second law?
cards.back: They transfer heat to their surroundings, increasing the surroundings' entropy more than their own order decreases it.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/06 Basic Principles of Physical Chemistry/13 Entropy and spontaneous reactions

cards.front: In an exothermic reaction, what happens to the entropy of the surroundings?
cards.back: It increases, because energy is transferred to them as heat.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/06 Basic Principles of Physical Chemistry/13 Entropy and spontaneous reactions

cards.front: Write the Gibbs free energy equation.
cards.back: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/06 Basic Principles of Physical Chemistry/14 Gibbs free energy

cards.front: What does a negative ΔG tell you?
cards.back: The reaction is exergonic and can be spontaneous; the products have less free energy than the reactants.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/06 Basic Principles of Physical Chemistry/14 Gibbs free energy

cards.front: What is an endergonic reaction?
cards.back: One with positive ΔG, which needs an input of energy and does not happen spontaneously.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/06 Basic Principles of Physical Chemistry/14 Gibbs free energy

cards.front: In ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, what unit must T be in?
cards.back: Kelvin.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/06 Basic Principles of Physical Chemistry/14 Gibbs free energy

cards.front: Why can glucose be phosphorylated by ATP but not directly by phosphate?
cards.back: Glucose + Pᵢ has a positive ΔG; coupling it to ATP hydrolysis, which has a large negative ΔG, makes the total ΔG negative.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/06 Basic Principles of Physical Chemistry/15 Coupling biochemical reactions

cards.front: Write the rule for ΔG of a coupled reaction.
cards.back: ΔG3 = ΔG1 + ΔG2, and it must be negative.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/06 Basic Principles of Physical Chemistry/15 Coupling biochemical reactions

cards.front: Which enzyme couples ATP hydrolysis to glucose phosphorylation?
cards.back: Hexokinase.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/06 Basic Principles of Physical Chemistry/15 Coupling biochemical reactions

cards.front: What does the double arrow ⇌ show?
cards.back: The reaction is reversible: the forward and reverse reactions both happen.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/07 Chemical Energy and Equilibria/01 Reversible reactions

cards.front: Do most biological reactions go to completion?
cards.back: No. Products re-form reactants, so they reach an equilibrium instead.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/07 Chemical Energy and Equilibria/01 Reversible reactions

cards.front: What is true of the forward and back rates at equilibrium?
cards.back: They are equal.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/07 Chemical Energy and Equilibria/02 Reaching dynamic equilibrium

cards.front: Why is chemical equilibrium called dynamic?
cards.back: Both forward and back reactions continue, but at equal rates, so there is no net change.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/07 Chemical Energy and Equilibria/02 Reaching dynamic equilibrium

cards.front: What does d[X]/dt = 0 mean?
cards.back: The concentration of each species no longer changes with time.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/07 Chemical Energy and Equilibria/02 Reaching dynamic equilibrium

cards.front: At t = 0, why can only the forward reaction occur?
cards.back: No products (C and D) are present yet.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/07 Chemical Energy and Equilibria/02 Reaching dynamic equilibrium

cards.front: Write Kc for aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD.
cards.back: Kc = [C]ᶜ[D]ᵈ / [A]ᵃ[B]ᵇ.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/07 Chemical Energy and Equilibria/03 The equilibrium constant K

cards.front: What happens to the stoichiometric coefficients in a K expression?
cards.back: They become the powers the concentrations are raised to.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/07 Chemical Energy and Equilibria/03 The equilibrium constant K

cards.front: A reaction has K = 10⁵. Where does the equilibrium lie?
cards.back: Far to the right: products dominate.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/07 Chemical Energy and Equilibria/03 The equilibrium constant K

cards.front: Write K for N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃.
cards.back: K = [NH₃]² / [N₂][H₂]³.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/07 Chemical Energy and Equilibria/03 The equilibrium constant K

cards.front: Write Kd for PL ⇌ P + L.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/07 Chemical Energy and Equilibria/04 Binding equilibria and Kd

cards.front: A drug has a very small Kd for its receptor. Does it bind strongly or weakly?
cards.back: Strongly: little of the complex dissociates.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/07 Chemical Energy and Equilibria/04 Binding equilibria and Kd

cards.front: For a strong protein–ligand interaction, which reaction is favourable?
cards.back: Association.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/07 Chemical Energy and Equilibria/04 Binding equilibria and Kd

cards.front: Ab and P start at 1 M each and K = 1000 M⁻¹. Write the expression for K in terms of x.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/07 Chemical Energy and Equilibria/05 Using equilibrium constants

cards.front: In the antibody example, why is the root x ≈ 1.03 M rejected?
cards.back: x cannot be bigger than the 1 M of antibody and protein you started with.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/07 Chemical Energy and Equilibria/05 Using equilibrium constants

cards.front: What are the equilibrium concentrations in the antibody example?
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/07 Chemical Energy and Equilibria/05 Using equilibrium constants

cards.front: State Le Chatelier's principle.
cards.back: When a system at equilibrium is disturbed, its composition adjusts to minimise the effect of the disturbance.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/07 Chemical Energy and Equilibria/06 Le Chatelier's principle

cards.front: Raising the temperature favours which direction of a reaction?
cards.back: The endothermic direction.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/07 Chemical Energy and Equilibria/06 Le Chatelier's principle

cards.front: Does adding a catalyst change K?
cards.back: No. It speeds up the forward and back reactions equally, so equilibrium is reached faster but K is unchanged.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/07 Chemical Energy and Equilibria/06 Le Chatelier's principle

cards.front: You add more reactant to a reaction at equilibrium. Which way does it shift, and does Kc change?
cards.back: Forward, towards products; Kc stays the same once equilibrium is re-established.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/07 Chemical Energy and Equilibria/06 Le Chatelier's principle

cards.front: What is ΔrG at equilibrium?
cards.back: Zero: the minimum of the G against composition curve.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/07 Chemical Energy and Equilibria/07 Gibbs energy and equilibrium

cards.front: If ΔrG < 0, which way does the reaction go?
cards.back: Forward, towards products.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/07 Chemical Energy and Equilibria/07 Gibbs energy and equilibrium

cards.front: What does ΔrG represent on a graph of G against composition?
cards.back: The slope of the curve.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/07 Chemical Energy and Equilibria/07 Gibbs energy and equilibrium

cards.front: Write the van't Hoff isotherm.
cards.back: ΔrG° = −RT ln K.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/07 Chemical Energy and Equilibria/08 Linking ΔG and K, the van't Hoff isotherm

cards.front: At equilibrium, what are Q and ΔrG equal to?
cards.back: Q = K, and ΔrG = 0.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/07 Chemical Energy and Equilibria/08 Linking ΔG and K, the van't Hoff isotherm

cards.front: If K > 1, what is the sign of ΔG°?
cards.back: Negative: ln K is positive, so −RT ln K is negative.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/07 Chemical Energy and Equilibria/08 Linking ΔG and K, the van't Hoff isotherm

cards.front: What is the value of R, and what unit must T be in?
cards.back: 8.315 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹; T in kelvin.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/07 Chemical Energy and Equilibria/08 Linking ΔG and K, the van't Hoff isotherm

cards.front: An exothermic reaction has a positive ΔS. When is it spontaneous?
cards.back: At all temperatures.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/07 Chemical Energy and Equilibria/09 Enthalpy, entropy and spontaneity

cards.front: An endothermic reaction has a positive ΔS. When is K > 1?
cards.back: Only above T = ΔrH° / ΔrS°, at high temperature.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/07 Chemical Energy and Equilibria/09 Enthalpy, entropy and spontaneity

cards.front: Can an endothermic reaction with negative ΔS ever be spontaneous?
cards.back: No: ΔG is positive at every temperature.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/07 Chemical Energy and Equilibria/09 Enthalpy, entropy and spontaneity

cards.front: Can you predict the rate of a reaction from ΔG?
cards.back: No. ΔG shows whether a reaction is spontaneous, not how fast; rates are found by experiment.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/07 Chemical Energy and Equilibria/10 Reaction rates and orders

cards.front: For a first-order reaction, how does the rate depend on [A]?
cards.back: It is directly proportional to [A], and the half-life is constant.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/07 Chemical Energy and Equilibria/10 Reaction rates and orders

cards.front: What is the overall order for Rate = k[A]¹[B]²?
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/07 Chemical Energy and Equilibria/10 Reaction rates and orders

cards.front: What two conditions must a collision meet to cause a reaction?
cards.back: Enough energy and the correct orientation.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/07 Chemical Energy and Equilibria/11 Collision theory and activation energy

cards.front: Define activation energy.
cards.back: The minimum energy a reactant molecule must have for the reaction to proceed.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/07 Chemical Energy and Equilibria/11 Collision theory and activation energy

cards.front: Give three ways to increase reaction rate.
cards.back: Increase concentration, increase temperature, lower the activation energy.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/07 Chemical Energy and Equilibria/11 Collision theory and activation energy

cards.front: What is the transition state?
cards.back: The highest-energy species that exists during a reaction, marked ‡.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/07 Chemical Energy and Equilibria/11 Collision theory and activation energy

cards.front: How does a catalyst speed up a reaction?
cards.back: It provides an alternative route with a lower activation energy, or stabilises the transition state.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/07 Chemical Energy and Equilibria/12 Catalysts lower the activation energy

cards.front: Does a catalyst change the position of equilibrium?
cards.back: No. It only changes the rate, so K and ΔG are unchanged.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/07 Chemical Energy and Equilibria/12 Catalysts lower the activation energy

cards.front: Why are only small amounts of catalyst needed?
cards.back: It is not consumed; it is chemically unchanged at the end.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Biological Chemistry/Lectures/07 Chemical Energy and Equilibria/12 Catalysts lower the activation energy

cards.front: How does Biomedicine define its own field?
cards.back: The study of the molecular and cellular basis of human disease, and how that knowledge becomes diagnosis, monitoring, treatment and prevention.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Introduction to Biomedicine/Lectures/01 Introductory Lecture/01 What Biomedicine actually is

cards.front: What does Biomedicine translate its knowledge into?
cards.back: Diagnosis, monitoring, treatment and prevention of human disease.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Introduction to Biomedicine/Lectures/01 Introductory Lecture/01 What Biomedicine actually is

cards.front: What are the nine Grand Challenge themes?
cards.back: Infectious diseases and vaccinations; antibiotic resistance; microbiome and host disease risk; stem cells and biomedical engineering; curing cancer; ageing; nutrition, diet and health; obesity and eating disorders; and exploiting the human genome for personalised medicine.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Introduction to Biomedicine/Lectures/01 Introductory Lecture/02 The Grand Challenges in Biomedicine

cards.front: What happens in the autumn semester of this module?
cards.back: Grand Challenges lectures, a disease pathogenesis and treatment seminar series, and lectures on techniques for biomedical research.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Introduction to Biomedicine/Lectures/01 Introductory Lecture/03 How the year is structured

cards.front: How big is the Introduction to Biomedicine module, and how does it end?
cards.back: It is a year-long, 40-credit module. It closes with a Biomedicine symposium where students present their favourite aspect of biomedicine from the first year.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Introduction to Biomedicine/Lectures/01 Introductory Lecture/03 How the year is structured

cards.front: What are the two lecture series in the autumn semester?
cards.back: Grand Challenges in Biomedicine, and Techniques for Biomedical Research and Biomedical Science.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Introduction to Biomedicine/Lectures/01 Introductory Lecture/04 Autumn semester, the two lecture series

cards.front: Which Grand Challenge lectures fall in weeks 2 and 3, and what is week 6?
cards.back: Week 2 is infectious diseases and vaccinations and week 3 is antibiotic resistance. Week 6 is an independent learning week.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Introduction to Biomedicine/Lectures/01 Introductory Lecture/04 Autumn semester, the two lecture series

cards.front: How big are the seminar groups and who leads them?
cards.back: 6 to 8 students, with a faculty seminar leader who is an expert in that biomedical field.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Introduction to Biomedicine/Lectures/01 Introductory Lecture/05 The seminar series, disease pathogenesis and treatment

cards.front: What is week 8 of the seminar series for?
cards.back: A dedicated troubleshooting and de-brief workshop.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Introduction to Biomedicine/Lectures/01 Introductory Lecture/05 The seminar series, disease pathogenesis and treatment

cards.front: What happens in the spring semester of this module?
cards.back: Practical classes in biomedical research techniques, the drug development pipeline, and clinical diagnosis lectures from NNUH biomedical scientists.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Introduction to Biomedicine/Lectures/01 Introductory Lecture/06 Spring semester, three more lecture series, plus practicals

cards.front: Who gives the laboratory medicine lectures in the spring semester?
cards.back: Biomedical scientists from the Norfolk and Norwich University Hospital.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Introduction to Biomedicine/Lectures/01 Introductory Lecture/06 Spring semester, three more lecture series, plus practicals

cards.front: What are the spring practical classes for?
cards.back: Hands-on experience of the techniques described in the autumn semester, applied to a biomedical research problem.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Introduction to Biomedicine/Lectures/01 Introductory Lecture/06 Spring semester, three more lecture series, plus practicals

cards.front: How many seminar topics are offered, and how do you choose one?
cards.back: Eleven. Students email their top 3 choices to the module organiser.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Introduction to Biomedicine/Lectures/01 Introductory Lecture/07 Seminar topics (Introductory Lecture)

cards.front: Name four of the eleven seminar topics.
cards.back: For example: stem cells for tendon regeneration, biomedical application of stem cells, skin in health and disease, pharmacology of glaucoma, congenital diseases, personalized medicine, will we ever cure cancer, why does menopause exist, the placenta in pregnancy complications, Alzheimer's disease, and experimental models in Cystic Fibrosis drug development.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Introduction to Biomedicine/Lectures/01 Introductory Lecture/07 Seminar topics (Introductory Lecture)

cards.front: What's the difference between an infectious, a communicable, and a zoonotic disease?
cards.back: Infectious: caused by a pathogenic microorganism. Communicable: an infectious disease spread person to person. Zoonotic: an animal infectious disease that can transmit to humans.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Introduction to Biomedicine/Lectures/02 Infectious Diseases and Vaccinations/01 What an infectious disease actually is

cards.front: Which four groups of microorganism can cause infectious disease?
cards.back: Bacteria, viruses, fungi and parasites.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Introduction to Biomedicine/Lectures/02 Infectious Diseases and Vaccinations/01 What an infectious disease actually is

cards.front: What's the difference between an outbreak/epidemic and a pandemic?
cards.back: An outbreak/epidemic is a sudden increase in cases above what's normally expected in one population and area. A pandemic is an epidemic that has spread across multiple countries or continents.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Introduction to Biomedicine/Lectures/02 Infectious Diseases and Vaccinations/02 Infectious disease terms, endemic to pandemic

cards.front: What does 'endemic' mean?
cards.back: The amount of a particular disease that is usually present in a community, i.e. its baseline level, not a sudden increase.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Introduction to Biomedicine/Lectures/02 Infectious Diseases and Vaccinations/02 Infectious disease terms, endemic to pandemic

cards.front: Give an example of a disease spread by each route: airborne, bodily fluids, arthropods and soil.
cards.back: Airborne: influenza or tuberculosis. Bodily fluids: hepatitis B or Ebola. Arthropods: malaria (mosquitoes) or Lyme disease (ticks). Soil: tetanus or anthrax.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Introduction to Biomedicine/Lectures/02 Infectious Diseases and Vaccinations/03 How infectious diseases spread

cards.front: By which routes can HIV spread?
cards.back: Sexual transmission, and from mother to child.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Introduction to Biomedicine/Lectures/02 Infectious Diseases and Vaccinations/03 How infectious diseases spread

cards.front: Name a disease spread through food and one spread through water.
cards.back: Food: salmonellosis or listeriosis. Water: cholera.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Introduction to Biomedicine/Lectures/02 Infectious Diseases and Vaccinations/03 How infectious diseases spread

cards.front: What are the 'big three' infectious diseases, and roughly how many people do they affect?
cards.back: TB (~10 million ill, 1.4 million deaths in 2019), HIV (37.6 million living with it in 2020), Malaria (229 million cases, 409,000 deaths in 2019).
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Introduction to Biomedicine/Lectures/02 Infectious Diseases and Vaccinations/04 Why this is a Grand Challenge

cards.front: Why do infectious diseases hit low-income countries harder?
cards.back: 6 of the leading causes of death in low-income countries are communicable diseases, versus only 2 in high-income countries.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Introduction to Biomedicine/Lectures/02 Infectious Diseases and Vaccinations/04 Why this is a Grand Challenge

cards.front: Which 3 infectious diseases appear in the WHO's top 10 global causes of death (as opposed to the 'big three')?
cards.back: COVID-19, lower respiratory infections, and tuberculosis. Note this is a different list from the 'big three' (TB, HIV, Malaria), which are the three biggest infectious disease burdens specifically, not the overall top 10 causes of death.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Introduction to Biomedicine/Lectures/02 Infectious Diseases and Vaccinations/04 Why this is a Grand Challenge

cards.front: Name the 5 main bacterial cell shapes.
cards.back: Bacillus (rods), Coccus (spherical), Filamentous, Spirillum (loose spiral), Spirochete (tightly coiled/corkscrew).
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Introduction to Biomedicine/Lectures/02 Infectious Diseases and Vaccinations/05 Microorganisms, bacteria

cards.front: What's the key structural difference between Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria?
cards.back: Gram-positive cells have several thick layers of peptidoglycan and retain crystal violet stain (purple). Gram-negative cells have a thinner peptidoglycan layer plus an outer membrane, lose the stain, and appear pink when counterstained with safranin.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Introduction to Biomedicine/Lectures/02 Infectious Diseases and Vaccinations/05 Microorganisms, bacteria

cards.front: Why are viruses not considered to be alive?
cards.back: They're obligate intracellular parasites: they can only replicate inside a host cell, relying on it for energy, metabolic intermediates and protein synthesis.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Introduction to Biomedicine/Lectures/02 Infectious Diseases and Vaccinations/06 Microorganisms, viruses

cards.front: What's the difference between a naked virus and an enveloped virus?
cards.back: A naked virus has just a protein capsid (mainly infects bacteria). An enveloped virus has a capsid plus an outer phospholipid envelope derived from the host cell (mainly infects animals).
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Introduction to Biomedicine/Lectures/02 Infectious Diseases and Vaccinations/06 Microorganisms, viruses

cards.front: Name the four outcomes a virus can have once inside a host cell.
cards.back: Lytic infection (replicates and destroys the host cell), persistent infection (replicates and buds out without destroying the cell), latent infection (viral DNA present but not replicating), and transformation (converts the host cell into a tumour cell).
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Introduction to Biomedicine/Lectures/02 Infectious Diseases and Vaccinations/06 Microorganisms, viruses

cards.front: Are most fungi harmful to humans? Who is most at risk from fungal infections?
cards.back: No. Most are harmless and only a few cause disease (for example athlete's foot and ringworm). Fungal infections can become serious in immune-compromised people, such as with HIV/AIDS or during cancer treatment.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Introduction to Biomedicine/Lectures/02 Infectious Diseases and Vaccinations/07 Microorganisms, fungi and parasites

cards.front: Give two ways fungi benefit humans.
cards.back: Fermentation (yeast for bread and beer) and antibiotics such as penicillin.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Introduction to Biomedicine/Lectures/02 Infectious Diseases and Vaccinations/07 Microorganisms, fungi and parasites

cards.front: What is parasitism, and what is an example of a parasitic disease?
cards.back: A symbiotic relationship in which the parasite gets essential nutrients from the host, usually causing disease. Examples: malaria (from the female mosquito) and toxoplasmosis (from cats).
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Introduction to Biomedicine/Lectures/02 Infectious Diseases and Vaccinations/07 Microorganisms, fungi and parasites

cards.front: What's the single most common cause of pneumonia, and who is most at risk from it?
cards.back: The bacterium Streptococcus pneumoniae. Most at risk: babies and young children, the elderly, and those with weakened immune systems or pre-existing illness.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Introduction to Biomedicine/Lectures/02 Infectious Diseases and Vaccinations/08 Case study, pneumonia

cards.front: What happens in the lungs in pneumonia?
cards.back: The air sacs (alveoli) in one or both lungs become inflamed and fill with fluid, making it difficult to breathe.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Introduction to Biomedicine/Lectures/02 Infectious Diseases and Vaccinations/08 Case study, pneumonia

cards.front: How big a cause of child deaths is pneumonia?
cards.back: It is the single largest infectious cause of death in children worldwide: 15% of all deaths in under-5s (808,694 child deaths in 2017).
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Introduction to Biomedicine/Lectures/02 Infectious Diseases and Vaccinations/08 Case study, pneumonia

cards.front: How is pneumonia prevented?
cards.back: Vaccination against Streptococcus pneumoniae and against flu (a risk factor for pneumonia), plus improved nutrition, housing and hygiene.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Introduction to Biomedicine/Lectures/02 Infectious Diseases and Vaccinations/08 Case study, pneumonia

cards.front: Which immune cell surface receptor does HIV target, and what cell types display it?
cards.back: The CD4 receptor, found on T-cells, macrophages, and monocytes.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Introduction to Biomedicine/Lectures/02 Infectious Diseases and Vaccinations/09 Case study, HIV and AIDS

cards.front: What are the stages of HIV disease progression without treatment?
cards.back: Acute infection (flu-like symptoms, high viral load) then chronic infection (low-level multiplication, asymptomatic, immune system eventually overwhelmed) then AIDS (immune system can no longer fight opportunistic infections; typical survival without treatment is about 3 years).
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Introduction to Biomedicine/Lectures/02 Infectious Diseases and Vaccinations/09 Case study, HIV and AIDS

cards.front: What is HAART, and what does it actually do?
cards.back: Highly active anti-retroviral therapy: 3 or more antiretroviral drugs aiming to reduce HIV viral load to undetectable levels. It doesn't cure HIV, but suppresses it and lets the immune system recover.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Introduction to Biomedicine/Lectures/02 Infectious Diseases and Vaccinations/09 Case study, HIV and AIDS

cards.front: What does vaccination actually do, and what's its estimated global impact?
cards.back: Deliberate exposure to a preparation from an infectious agent to induce immunity. Saves an estimated 2 to 3 million lives globally each year.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Introduction to Biomedicine/Lectures/02 Infectious Diseases and Vaccinations/10 Vaccination, approaches

cards.front: What are the three general approaches to vaccine design?
cards.back: Whole microbe approach (live-attenuated, inactivated, or recombinant vector), subunit approach (using part of the microorganism, e.g. protein or sugar), and genetic approach (DNA or mRNA, where host cells produce the immunogenic protein themselves).
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Introduction to Biomedicine/Lectures/02 Infectious Diseases and Vaccinations/10 Vaccination, approaches

cards.front: What's the difference between disease eradication and disease elimination? Give an example of each.
cards.back: Eradication is a complete, permanent, worldwide reduction to zero new cases, with no further control measures needed (e.g. smallpox). Elimination is reduction to zero or a very low rate within a defined area, but continued measures are still needed to prevent it re-establishing (e.g. measles).
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Introduction to Biomedicine/Lectures/02 Infectious Diseases and Vaccinations/11 Vaccination, success stories

cards.front: What ratio did Mendel observe in the F2 pea generation for tall:dwarf?
cards.back: Approximately 3:1 (tall:dwarf).
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/01 Heredity and DNA/01 Genetics, from Mendel to chromosomes

cards.front: What did Griffith's experiment show?
cards.back: Live IIR plus heat-killed IIIS together kills the mouse and produces living IIIS bacteria. Something from the dead bacteria transformed the harmless ones. He called it the transforming principle.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/01 Heredity and DNA/02 Proving DNA is the hereditary material

cards.front: How did Avery, MacLeod and McCarty identify the transforming principle as DNA?
cards.back: Only the DNase-treated batch of IIIS filtrate failed to transform IIR cells. RNase and protease treatment didn't stop transformation. By elimination, DNA is the active factor.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/01 Heredity and DNA/02 Proving DNA is the hereditary material

cards.front: What isotopes did Hershey and Chase use, and why?
cards.back: ³²P labels DNA (phosphorus is in the DNA backbone, not protein). ³⁵S labels protein (sulfur is in cysteine and methionine, not DNA). After infection and blending, ³²P was inside the bacteria in the pellet and passed to progeny phage; ³⁵S stayed outside with the empty phage coats. So DNA is what enters the cell and carries the genetic information.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/01 Heredity and DNA/02 Proving DNA is the hereditary material

cards.front: Why does CaCl₂ make E. coli 'competent'?
cards.back: It provides positive ions that neutralise the negative charge on both the cell membrane and DNA's phosphate backbone, reducing repulsion so DNA can approach the cell.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/01 Heredity and DNA/03 Transformation in the lab

cards.front: What does the pGLO experiment demonstrate?
cards.back: That foreign DNA (a jellyfish GFP gene) was taken up by E. coli and actively expressed. The bacteria glow green under UV.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/01 Heredity and DNA/03 Transformation in the lab

cards.front: What is T-DNA, and what does Agrobacterium do with it?
cards.back: T-DNA is the segment of the Ti plasmid that gets physically transferred into a plant cell's genome during infection, hijacking its growth to form a gall.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/01 Heredity and DNA/04 Natural transformation

cards.front: At what wavelength do DNA and RNA absorb UV light most strongly, and what is that used for?
cards.back: 260 nm, because of the bases. It is the standard way to measure nucleic acid concentration and purity.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/01 Heredity and DNA/05 Physical and chemical properties of DNA and RNA

cards.front: What is denaturation of DNA, and what does it leave intact?
cards.back: Separating the two strands by breaking the hydrogen bonds between bases (using heat or chemicals). The covalent sugar-phosphate backbone stays intact.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/01 Heredity and DNA/05 Physical and chemical properties of DNA and RNA

cards.front: What is the hyperchromic effect?
cards.back: UV absorbance at 260 nm increases as DNA denatures, because unstacked single-stranded bases absorb more UV than stacked double-stranded ones.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/01 Heredity and DNA/05 Physical and chemical properties of DNA and RNA

cards.front: What is melting temperature (Tm), and why does more G and C raise it?
cards.back: The temperature at which half the DNA sample is denatured. G≡C pairs have 3 hydrogen bonds, which take more energy to break than the 2 in A=T.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/01 Heredity and DNA/05 Physical and chemical properties of DNA and RNA

cards.front: What is molecular hybridization?
cards.back: Complementary single strands from different sources re-annealing and base-pairing with each other. It is the principle behind PCR, probes and primers.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/01 Heredity and DNA/05 Physical and chemical properties of DNA and RNA

cards.front: What enzyme does the Le gene encode, and what happens in the dwarf mutant?
cards.back: Gibberellin 3β-hydroxylase. The mutant (le) has an A→G DNA change causing an ala229→thr amino acid swap, crippling the enzyme and reducing the height-promoting hormone.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/01 Heredity and DNA/06 Perspectives, where inheritance gets stranger

cards.front: What three parts make up a nucleotide?
cards.back: A 5-carbon sugar, a phosphate group, and a nitrogenous base.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/02 Structure of DNA and RNA/01 The nucleotide, DNA and RNA's shared building block

cards.front: What's the chemical difference between ribose and deoxyribose?
cards.back: Ribose has an -OH group on its 2′ carbon; deoxyribose has just -H there instead.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/02 Structure of DNA and RNA/01 The nucleotide, DNA and RNA's shared building block

cards.front: Name the two purines and three pyrimidines.
cards.back: Purines: Adenine, Guanine. Pyrimidines: Cytosine, Thymine (DNA only), Uracil (RNA only).
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/02 Structure of DNA and RNA/01 The nucleotide, DNA and RNA's shared building block

cards.front: What bond links nucleotides together, and between which carbons?
cards.back: A phosphodiester bond, between the 5′ carbon of one sugar and the 3′ carbon of the next.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/02 Structure of DNA and RNA/02 Linking nucleotides, the phosphodiester bond

cards.front: What direction is DNA/RNA always synthesised, transcribed, and translated in?
cards.back: 5′ to 3′, in all three processes.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/02 Structure of DNA and RNA/02 Linking nucleotides, the phosphodiester bond

cards.front: What did Rosalind Franklin's X-ray diffraction photographs show?
cards.back: They distinguished A-form from B-form DNA and suggested the molecule was probably helical. Watson and Crick used this data, shared via Maurice Wilkins, to build the double-helix model in 1953.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/02 Structure of DNA and RNA/03 Discovering the structure, Franklin, Chargaff, Watson and Crick

cards.front: What is Chargaff's rule, and why was it an important clue?
cards.back: %A is roughly equal to %T and %G roughly equal to %C in every species, even though the overall A+T versus G+C ratio varies widely. It was a direct clue toward complementary base pairing.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/02 Structure of DNA and RNA/03 Discovering the structure, Franklin, Chargaff, Watson and Crick

cards.front: Sarcina DNA is about 13% A and 37% G. What does that show about Chargaff's rule?
cards.back: A is still roughly equal to T (13.4 and 12.4) and G equal to C (37.1 and 37.1), even though the balance of A+T to G+C is very different from other species.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/02 Structure of DNA and RNA/03 Discovering the structure, Franklin, Chargaff, Watson and Crick

cards.front: How many hydrogen bonds hold A=T together, vs G≡C?
cards.back: A=T: 2 hydrogen bonds. G≡C: 3 hydrogen bonds.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/02 Structure of DNA and RNA/04 The double helix, full structure

cards.front: What does 'antiparallel' mean for the two DNA strands?
cards.back: One strand runs 5′→3′, the other runs 3′→5′: opposite directions.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/02 Structure of DNA and RNA/04 The double helix, full structure

cards.front: What are the double helix's key dimensions?
cards.back: 2 nm diameter, 0.34 nm rise per base pair, ~10 (precisely 10.4) base pairs per turn.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/02 Structure of DNA and RNA/04 The double helix, full structure

cards.front: Why does the major groove matter more than the minor groove for protein binding?
cards.back: The major groove exposes more of each base pair's distinguishing chemical detail, making it the site where sequence-reading proteins (e.g. transcription factors) typically bind.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/02 Structure of DNA and RNA/04 The double helix, full structure

cards.front: What are the three main types of RNA and their roles?
cards.back: mRNA carries the genetic message, tRNA delivers amino acids to ribosomes, rRNA is a structural and functional component of ribosomes.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/02 Structure of DNA and RNA/05 RNA, structure and the three main types

cards.front: tRNA is made single-stranded. Why does it still contain double-stranded regions?
cards.back: It folds back on itself, and complementary base pairing within the same molecule forms the double-stranded regions.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/02 Structure of DNA and RNA/05 RNA, structure and the three main types

cards.front: State the central dogma of molecular biology.
cards.back: Information flows one-way: DNA → RNA → protein. It cannot flow back from protein to nucleic acid.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/02 Structure of DNA and RNA/06 The central dogma

cards.front: What does the central dogma say can never happen?
cards.back: Information can pass between nucleic acids and from nucleic acid to protein, but never back from protein to nucleic acid or to another protein (Crick, 1970).
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/02 Structure of DNA and RNA/06 The central dogma

cards.front: What are the three theoretical models for how DNA could replicate, and which one is correct?
cards.back: Conservative (both parental strands stay together), semiconservative (each daughter has one parental and one new strand), and dispersive (parental and new DNA mixed throughout). Semiconservative is correct.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/03 DNA Replication/01 Three theoretical ways DNA could replicate

cards.front: How did Meselson and Stahl's experiment distinguish between the three replication models?
cards.back: They grew E. coli in heavy (¹⁵N) nitrogen medium, switched them to light (¹⁴N) medium, then used density gradient centrifugation to separate DNA by weight across successive generations.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/03 DNA Replication/02 The Meselson-Stahl experiment

cards.front: What banding pattern did Meselson and Stahl actually observe, and why did it confirm semiconservative replication?
cards.back: Generation 0 gave one heavy band; Generation I gave one intermediate band; Generation II gave one intermediate and one light band. This matches semiconservative replication exactly, since each new duplex should contain one old (heavy) and one new (light) strand.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/03 DNA Replication/02 The Meselson-Stahl experiment

cards.front: Which enzyme does most of the DNA synthesis in E. coli?
cards.back: DNA polymerase III, with DNA polymerase I playing a lesser role.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/03 DNA Replication/04 How new nucleotides get added

cards.front: What decides which base is added opposite a base on the parental strand?
cards.back: The parental strand is the template: it determines which base is incorporated opposite it into the new strand.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/03 DNA Replication/04 How new nucleotides get added

cards.front: How does a new nucleotide join the growing DNA chain?
cards.back: The incoming nucleotide (a dNTP, carrying three phosphates) attaches its 5′ end to the free 3′-OH end of the growing chain, releasing a pyrophosphate.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/03 DNA Replication/04 How new nucleotides get added

cards.front: Why can't DNA polymerase start building a new strand from scratch?
cards.back: It can only add nucleotides onto an existing free 3′ end. Primase first makes a short RNA primer to provide that starting point.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/03 DNA Replication/05 Starting a new strand, primers

cards.front: What did electron microscope images of replicating E. coli DNA show?
cards.back: The replication bubble gets bigger as replication proceeds. It is direct physical evidence that replication spreads outward from a starting point.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/03 DNA Replication/06 Visualising replication, the growing bubble

cards.front: What's the difference between the leading strand and the lagging strand?
cards.back: The leading strand is synthesised continuously in the same direction the replication fork moves. The lagging strand is synthesised discontinuously, in short Okazaki fragments, running in the opposite direction to fork movement.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/03 DNA Replication/07 Replication forks, leading and lagging strands

cards.front: Name the six key enzymes/proteins in E. coli DNA replication and what each one does.
cards.back: Helicase (DnaB): unwinds the helix. Primase: makes the RNA primer. DNA polymerase III: does most of the actual DNA synthesis. DNA polymerase I: removes RNA primers and replaces them with DNA. Ligase: joins Okazaki fragments together. DNA gyrase: removes supercoiling ahead of the fork.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/03 DNA Replication/08 The enzymes of replication

cards.front: Which enzyme removes the RNA primers, and which seals the gaps between Okazaki fragments?
cards.back: DNA polymerase I removes the primers and replaces them with DNA. DNA ligase seals the phosphodiester bonds joining the Okazaki fragments.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/03 DNA Replication/08 The enzymes of replication

cards.front: What does DNA gyrase do?
cards.back: It is a topoisomerase that removes the supercoiling caused by unwinding the helix ahead of the fork.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/03 DNA Replication/08 The enzymes of replication

cards.front: What is oriC, and what does it consist of?
cards.back: The E. coli chromosomal origin of replication: 245 bp, containing three repeats of a 13 bp sequence and four repeats of a 9 bp sequence.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/03 DNA Replication/09 Origins of replication, oriC

cards.front: Describe the three stages of initiation at oriC.
cards.back: (a) Around 20 DnaA proteins, each bound to ATP, bind the four 9 bp repeats and wrap the DNA around the complex. (b) The three 13 bp repeats are denatured in sequence. (c) DnaB helicase hexamers, helped by DnaC, bind each strand and start unwinding, ready for priming and synthesis.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/03 DNA Replication/09 Origins of replication, oriC

cards.front: How does replication terminate in E. coli?
cards.back: The two replication forks, moving in opposite directions from the single origin, meet at a terminus region containing Ter sequences. These are bound by the Tus protein, which arrests a fork approaching from one particular direction only (a 'fork trap').
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/03 DNA Replication/10 Termination of replication

cards.front: How does eukaryotic DNA replication differ from bacterial replication in terms of origins?
cards.back: Eukaryotes replicate from many origins at once (replicons of roughly 40 to 100 kbp each), rather than the single origin bacterial chromosomes use, since eukaryotic chromosomes are far larger.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/03 DNA Replication/11 Eukaryotic replication, multiple origins

cards.front: What problem does telomerase solve, and how?
cards.back: Because of how lagging-strand synthesis works, a linear chromosome would lose a little DNA from its ends with every round of replication. Telomerase solves this by adding new repeat sequences onto the chromosome ends, using its own internal RNA template.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/03 DNA Replication/12 Replication of chromosome ends, telomeres

cards.front: What happens in transcription and in translation?
cards.back: Transcription copies the DNA sequence into mRNA. Translation reads the mRNA codons on ribosomes, and the order of codons sets the order of amino acids in the protein.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/05 The Genetic Code/01 Information flow, DNA to mRNA to protein

cards.front: Why must the genetic code be read in triplets?
cards.back: DNA has 4 bases. Singles give 4 combinations and pairs give 16, too few for 20 amino acids. Triplets give 4 × 4 × 4 = 64 codons, enough with redundancy (Brenner).
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/05 The Genetic Code/02 Why the code must be a triplet

cards.front: What did Crick's frameshift experiments in phage T4 rII show?
cards.back: Inserting or deleting 1 or 2 nucleotides abolished gene function, but 3 often did not, because three restores the reading frame. So the code is read in triplets.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/05 The Genetic Code/03 Proving the triplet code, frameshift mutations

cards.front: What was in Nirenberg and Matthaei's cell-free system?
cards.back: An RNA polymer (e.g. poly-U), tRNAs each coupled to a radioactive amino acid, ribosomes, and an energy source (GTP). Protein was precipitated with acetone and its radioactivity measured.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/05 The Genetic Code/04 Cracking the code, Nirenberg and Matthaei

cards.front: What did the poly-U experiment show, and how was the RNA made?
cards.back: Poly-U gave about 39,800 counts/min of phenylalanine in protein versus about 40 to 50 for poly-A, poly-C or none, so UUU = phenylalanine. The RNA was made with polynucleotide phosphorylase, which needs no DNA template.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/05 The Genetic Code/04 Cracking the code, Nirenberg and Matthaei

cards.front: How did Khorana's repeating copolymers assign codons? Give an example.
cards.back: A repeat read in different frames gives a known set of codons. Repeating UC gives UCU and CUC, and the product contained leucine and serine.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/05 The Genetic Code/05 Repeating copolymers, Khorana

cards.front: Which codons did Khorana's GUA, GAU and GUAA repeats reveal?
cards.back: The stop codons UAA, UAG and UGA: these repeats did not prime synthesis of a polypeptide product.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/05 The Genetic Code/05 Repeating copolymers, Khorana

cards.front: What does it mean that the genetic code is redundant?
cards.back: 64 codons: 61 encode the 20 amino acids and 3 are stops, so most amino acids have several codons, which usually differ at the third base (e.g. valine: GUU, GUC, GUA, GUG).
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/05 The Genetic Code/06 The code is redundant

cards.front: What is the wobble hypothesis?
cards.back: Crick's proposal that the first two codon bases pair strictly with the tRNA, but pairing at the third base is less constrained and can break standard rules, so one tRNA can read more than one codon.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/05 The Genetic Code/07 The wobble hypothesis

cards.front: What is the start codon, and what is the first amino acid in bacteria?
cards.back: AUG, which encodes methionine. In bacteria the first amino acid is the modified form N-formylmethionine (fMet).
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/05 The Genetic Code/08 Start and stop, AUG and the stop codons

cards.front: mRNA 5′-UGAUUCCUAGGAGGUUUGACCUAUGCGAUCUGUUGGU-3′ has one start codon. What are the first five amino acids?
cards.back: Met, Arg, Ser, Val, Gly: reading from AUG gives AUG CGA UCU GUU GGU.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/05 The Genetic Code/08 Start and stop, AUG and the stop codons

cards.front: Which peptide starts at the AUG in 5′-UCGGGUGUCGAUACGCUGGUGUCAAAUAUGCUUUUGCCAAUU-3′?
cards.back: Met, Leu, Leu, Pro, Ile: AUG CUU UUG CCA AUU.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/05 The Genetic Code/08 Start and stop, AUG and the stop codons

cards.front: What do 'non-overlapping' and 'commaless' mean for the genetic code?
cards.back: Non-overlapping: each nucleotide is part of only one codon. Commaless: codons are read one after the other with no gaps between them.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/05 The Genetic Code/09 Non-overlapping and commaless

cards.front: Why is the genetic code only 'nearly' universal?
cards.back: In some proteins in some species, UGA encodes selenocysteine (cysteine with selenium for sulphur) and UAG encodes pyrrolysine (lysine plus a pyrroline group).
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/05 The Genetic Code/10 A (nearly) universal code, selenocysteine and pyrrolysine

cards.front: Which DNA strand does RNA polymerase read, and which strand does the mRNA match?
cards.back: It reads the template strand. The mRNA is complementary to the template and has the same sequence as the coding strand, with U in place of T.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/06 Transcription/01 Transcription, making an RNA copy of DNA

cards.front: A coding strand reads 5′-ATGCTTTTGCCAATT-3′. What is the mRNA and the peptide?
cards.back: mRNA 5′-AUGCUUUUGCCAAUU-3′, read as AUG CUU UUG CCA AUU: Met, Leu, Leu, Pro, Ile.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/06 Transcription/01 Transcription, making an RNA copy of DNA

cards.front: What are the 5′ and 3′ UTRs?
cards.back: Untranslated regions of the mRNA: the 5′ UTR lies between the start of transcription and AUG, the 3′ UTR between the stop codon and the end of transcription.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/06 Transcription/02 Gene and mRNA structure

cards.front: What do 'cis-acting' and 'trans-acting' mean for a promoter and RNA polymerase?
cards.back: The promoter is cis-acting: a DNA sequence that only controls its own gene. RNA polymerase is trans-acting: a protein that can act on any matching promoter.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/06 Transcription/03 Prokaryotic promoters and RNA polymerase

cards.front: What are the subunits of E. coli RNA polymerase?
cards.back: 2 α, 1 β, 1 β′ and 1 σ (sigma) subunit.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/06 Transcription/03 Prokaryotic promoters and RNA polymerase

cards.front: What are the −10 and −35 consensus sequences of an E. coli promoter?
cards.back: −35: TTGACA. −10: TATAAT. They are 15 to 20 bp apart, and the −10 box is 5 to 9 bp before +1.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/06 Transcription/03 Prokaryotic promoters and RNA polymerase

cards.front: What does the sigma factor do?
cards.back: It binds the −10 and −35 boxes so RNA polymerase starts at the right place. Different sigma factors recognise different sets of promoters.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/06 Transcription/03 Prokaryotic promoters and RNA polymerase
