cards.front: How do intrinsic and extrinsic terminators differ?
cards.back: Intrinsic: the RNA forms a hairpin loop and polymerase and RNA are released. Extrinsic: the rho protein is needed to end transcription.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/06 Transcription/04 Termination of transcription

cards.front: What is an operon? Name the lac operon genes and their products.
cards.back: Linked genes under one promoter. lacZ: β-galactosidase (splits lactose). lacY: permease (brings lactose in). lacA: transacetylase.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/06 Transcription/06 The lac operon

cards.front: How does lactose switch on the lac operon?
cards.back: Without lactose the lacI repressor sits on the operator and blocks RNA polymerase. Lactose (strictly allolactose) binds the repressor so it releases the operator.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/06 Transcription/07 Repression and induction

cards.front: How does glucose control the lac operon?
cards.back: No glucose: cAMP rises, binds CAP, and cAMP-CAP binds next to the promoter to strongly activate transcription. With glucose, cAMP is low and activation is weak.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/06 Transcription/08 Glucose control, cAMP and CAP

cards.front: Lactose present, glucose present: what happens to lac gene expression and why?
cards.back: Low. The repressor is released, but with little cAMP, CAP does not activate, so transcription is weak.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/06 Transcription/08 Glucose control, cAMP and CAP

cards.front: What do lacI mutants that can't bind the operator, and operator Oᶜ mutants, have in common?
cards.back: Both give constitutive expression: the repressor can't block transcription, so the genes are always on.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/06 Transcription/09 lac operon mutants

cards.front: What happens with a lacI mutant whose repressor can't bind lactose?
cards.back: The operon stays repressed even with lactose present, because the repressor never leaves the operator.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/06 Transcription/09 lac operon mutants

cards.front: What is in a eukaryotic primary transcript, and which polymerase makes mRNA?
cards.back: Exons (coding) and introns (non-coding). RNA Pol II makes all protein-coding mRNAs and microRNAs.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/06 Transcription/10 Eukaryotic transcription, an overview

cards.front: How does transcription start in eukaryotes?
cards.back: Chromatin remodelling exposes the promoter, TBP binds the TATA box, TAFs help RNA Pol II bind to form the basal transcription complex, and transcription factors on enhancers boost initiation up to 100 times.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/06 Transcription/11 Starting eukaryotic transcription

cards.front: How is a eukaryotic mRNA capped and tailed?
cards.back: A G is added to the 5′ end by a 5′-5′ triphosphate link and methylated. The 3′ end is cut after AAUAAA and poly-A polymerase adds 100 to 200 A.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/06 Transcription/12 Capping and tailing

cards.front: What are the three key intron motifs, and what removes introns?
cards.back: Splice donor, branch site and splice acceptor. The spliceosome, which contains snRNPs that base pair with the intron, removes them.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/06 Transcription/13 Splicing

cards.front: What is alternative splicing and why does it matter?
cards.back: Joining exons in different combinations, so one gene gives several mRNAs and proteins: it generates protein diversity.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/06 Transcription/14 Alternative splicing

cards.front: Name the three tRNA sites on the ribosome and what each holds.
cards.back: A site: incoming aminoacyl-tRNA. P site: peptidyl-tRNA with the growing chain. E site: uncharged tRNA about to leave.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/07 Translation/02 The ribosome and its three tRNA sites

cards.front: What are the subunits of a bacterial ribosome?
cards.back: 70S overall: 30S small subunit and 50S large subunit.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/07 Translation/02 The ribosome and its three tRNA sites

cards.front: Which part of the ribosome catalyses peptide bond formation?
cards.back: The 23S rRNA of the large subunit (peptidyl transferase), so the ribosome is a ribozyme.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/07 Translation/03 Overview of translation

cards.front: After a peptide bond forms, where do the two tRNAs move?
cards.back: The ribosome shifts one codon: the P-site tRNA moves to the E site and the A-site tRNA, now carrying the chain, moves to the P site.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/07 Translation/03 Overview of translation

cards.front: What do aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases do, and how many are there?
cards.back: They attach each amino acid to its matching tRNAs (charging). There are 20, one per amino acid.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/07 Translation/04 Charging tRNAs

cards.front: Why does an organism need fewer than 61 tRNAs?
cards.back: Wobble at the third codon position lets one tRNA read more than one codon, so a minimum of 31 is enough.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/07 Translation/04 Charging tRNAs

cards.front: What is the Shine-Dalgarno sequence and what does it do?
cards.back: The ribosome binding site on bacterial mRNA (AGGAGG). It base pairs with the 16S rRNA to position the start codon AUG in the ribosome.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/07 Translation/05 Initiation of translation

cards.front: Which tRNA sits in the P site at the start, and what pairs with what?
cards.back: fMet-tRNA. Its UAC anticodon pairs with the AUG start codon.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/07 Translation/05 Initiation of translation

cards.front: Describe one cycle of elongation.
cards.back: A charged tRNA enters the A site with EF-Tu; a peptide bond joins the chain to its amino acid; the ribosome moves three nucleotides so the tRNAs shift to E and P, and the empty tRNA leaves.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/07 Translation/06 Elongation

cards.front: How fast and how accurate is translation in E. coli?
cards.back: About 15 amino acids per second, with about 1 error in 10,000 amino acids.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/07 Translation/06 Elongation

cards.front: What is a polyribosome?
cards.back: One mRNA being translated by several ribosomes at the same time.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/07 Translation/07 Polyribosomes

cards.front: Which release factors recognise which stop codons?
cards.back: RF1: UAA and UAG. RF2: UAA and UGA.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/07 Translation/08 Termination of translation

cards.front: How is the finished polypeptide released?
cards.back: The release factor triggers hydrolysis of the bond between the polypeptide and the P-site tRNA, so water is added instead of an amino acid.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/07 Translation/08 Termination of translation

cards.front: What does recombinant DNA technology do?
cards.back: Creates new combinations of DNA sequences from different sources (cloning), which can then be put into prokaryotic or eukaryotic host cells.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/08 Plasmids and Recombinant DNA/01 Recombinant DNA technology

cards.front: What two tools made recombinant DNA technology possible?
cards.back: Restriction enzymes to cut DNA, and cloning vectors (plasmids) to carry and replicate it.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/08 Plasmids and Recombinant DNA/01 Recombinant DNA technology

cards.front: What bond does a restriction enzyme cut?
cards.back: The phosphodiester bonds of the DNA backbone, on both strands.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/08 Plasmids and Recombinant DNA/02 Restriction enzymes

cards.front: How long are the most commonly used restriction sites?
cards.back: 4 or 6 bases.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/08 Plasmids and Recombinant DNA/02 Restriction enzymes

cards.front: On average, how often does a 4-base recognition site occur in random DNA?
cards.back: Once every 256 bp (4⁴).
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/08 Plasmids and Recombinant DNA/02 Restriction enzymes

cards.front: What does palindromic mean for a restriction site?
cards.back: The sequence reads the same on both strands when each is read 5′ → 3′, e.g. GAATTC.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/08 Plasmids and Recombinant DNA/02 Restriction enzymes

cards.front: What sequence does EcoRI recognise, and where does it cut?
cards.back: GAATTC, cutting between G and A (G^AATTC) on each strand, leaving sticky ends.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/08 Plasmids and Recombinant DNA/03 Common restriction enzymes and their ends

cards.front: Which enzyme in the lecture gives blunt ends?
cards.back: AluI (AG^CT), which cuts both strands at the same point.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/08 Plasmids and Recombinant DNA/03 Common restriction enzymes and their ends

cards.front: What is the difference between sticky and blunt ends?
cards.back: Sticky ends have short single-stranded overhangs from offset cuts; blunt ends have none because both strands are cut at the same point.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/08 Plasmids and Recombinant DNA/03 Common restriction enzymes and their ends

cards.front: Where does BamHI come from, and what is its site?
cards.back: Bacillus amyloliquefaciens; G^GATCC.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/08 Plasmids and Recombinant DNA/03 Common restriction enzymes and their ends

cards.front: What holds two sticky ends together before ligation?
cards.back: Hydrogen bonds between complementary bases in the overhangs.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/08 Plasmids and Recombinant DNA/04 Joining DNA with DNA ligase

cards.front: What does DNA ligase do in cloning?
cards.back: Seals the nicks in the backbone by forming phosphodiester bonds, covalently joining the fragments.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/08 Plasmids and Recombinant DNA/04 Joining DNA with DNA ligase

cards.front: Why must the insert and vector be cut with the same enzyme?
cards.back: So their sticky ends are complementary and can anneal.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/08 Plasmids and Recombinant DNA/04 Joining DNA with DNA ligase

cards.front: List four properties of a good cloning vector.
cards.back: Several restriction sites, independent replication in the host, a selectable marker gene, and easy isolation from the host cell.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/08 Plasmids and Recombinant DNA/05 DNA cloning vectors

cards.front: Why does a vector need a selectable marker?
cards.back: To distinguish host cells that have taken up the vector from those that have not.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/08 Plasmids and Recombinant DNA/05 DNA cloning vectors

cards.front: What is a plasmid?
cards.back: A small, circular, double-stranded DNA molecule in bacteria that replicates independently of the chromosome.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/08 Plasmids and Recombinant DNA/05 DNA cloning vectors

cards.front: Why is the polylinker placed inside the lacZ gene of pUC18?
cards.back: So inserting DNA disrupts lacZ, letting recombinant colonies be spotted as white on X-gal plates.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/08 Plasmids and Recombinant DNA/06 pUC18, a bacterial plasmid vector

cards.front: On an ampicillin + X-gal plate, which colonies carry recombinant plasmids?
cards.back: White colonies. Blue ones carry plasmids without an insert.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/08 Plasmids and Recombinant DNA/06 pUC18, a bacterial plasmid vector

cards.front: What is the role of the ampicillin resistance gene in pUC18?
cards.back: It is the selectable marker: only bacteria that took up the plasmid survive on ampicillin.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/08 Plasmids and Recombinant DNA/06 pUC18, a bacterial plasmid vector

cards.front: Put the cloning steps in order: transform, ligate, cut, select.
cards.back: Cut (vector and insert with the same enzyme), ligate, transform, select.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/08 Plasmids and Recombinant DNA/07 Cloning into bacterial plasmids

cards.front: How are recombinant plasmids put into bacteria?
cards.back: Transformation, e.g. calcium chloride with a heat shock, or electroporation.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/08 Plasmids and Recombinant DNA/07 Cloning into bacterial plasmids

cards.front: How are cells carrying recombinant plasmids found?
cards.back: By plating on medium containing an antibiotic and/or a colour indicator such as X-gal.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/08 Plasmids and Recombinant DNA/07 Cloning into bacterial plasmids

cards.front: What is the natural role of restriction enzymes?
cards.back: Innate immunity in bacteria: they cut the DNA of invading viruses (bacteriophage).
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/08 Plasmids and Recombinant DNA/08 Natural roles of molecular biology enzymes

cards.front: Why does a restriction enzyme not cut the bacterium's own DNA?
cards.back: The bacterium methylates its own recognition sites, which protects them.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/08 Plasmids and Recombinant DNA/08 Natural roles of molecular biology enzymes

cards.front: Give a natural job of DNA ligase.
cards.back: Sealing breaks in DNA during replication (joining Okazaki fragments), repair and recombination.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/08 Plasmids and Recombinant DNA/08 Natural roles of molecular biology enzymes

cards.front: Cutting a 7.0 kb fragment with HindIII gives 6.2 and 0.8 kb. How many HindIII sites are there?
cards.back: One, 0.8 kb from one end.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/08 Plasmids and Recombinant DNA/09 Restriction mapping of plasmids

cards.front: In the example, the double digest gives 5.8, 0.8 and 0.4 kb. Which model fits, and why?
cards.back: Model 1: HindIII at 0.8 and SalI at 1.2 kb from the same end gives 0.8, 0.4 and 5.8 kb. Model 2 would give 0.8, 5.0 and 1.2 kb.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/08 Plasmids and Recombinant DNA/09 Restriction mapping of plasmids

cards.front: Why is a double digest needed?
cards.back: Single digests give each site's distance from an end but not which end; the double digest shows how the sites lie relative to each other.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/08 Plasmids and Recombinant DNA/09 Restriction mapping of plasmids

cards.front: On a gel, which fragments travel furthest?
cards.back: The smallest.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/08 Plasmids and Recombinant DNA/09 Restriction mapping of plasmids

cards.front: Who developed PCR, and when?
cards.back: Kary Mullis in the 1980s; Nobel Prize in Chemistry 1993.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/10 Polymerase Chain Reaction/01 What PCR is

cards.front: List the five things needed to set up a PCR.
cards.back: Template DNA, two primers, dNTPs, buffer with magnesium, and a thermostable DNA polymerase.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/10 Polymerase Chain Reaction/02 Setting up a PCR

cards.front: How long are PCR primers, and where do they bind?
cards.back: About 20 nucleotides; to the sequences flanking each side of the region to be amplified, one on each strand.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/10 Polymerase Chain Reaction/02 Setting up a PCR

cards.front: Where does Taq polymerase come from?
cards.back: The heat-loving bacterium Thermus aquaticus.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/10 Polymerase Chain Reaction/02 Setting up a PCR

cards.front: Why must the DNA polymerase used in PCR be thermostable?
cards.back: Each cycle heats the reaction to about 95 °C, which would denature an ordinary polymerase.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/10 Polymerase Chain Reaction/03 DNA polymerases and fidelity

cards.front: What is the trade-off with high-fidelity polymerases?
cards.back: They are more accurate but more expensive and synthesise DNA more slowly.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/10 Polymerase Chain Reaction/03 DNA polymerases and fidelity

cards.front: Give the three steps of a PCR cycle with their temperatures.
cards.back: Denaturation at 92–95 °C, annealing at 50–65 °C, extension at about 72 °C.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/10 Polymerase Chain Reaction/04 The PCR cycle

cards.front: Which end of the primer does DNA polymerase extend?
cards.back: The 3′ end.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/10 Polymerase Chain Reaction/04 The PCR cycle

cards.front: How many cycles does a typical PCR run?
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/10 Polymerase Chain Reaction/04 The PCR cycle

cards.front: What does the first PCR cycle produce from one double-stranded molecule?
cards.back: Two double-stranded DNA molecules, each with a primer incorporated into the new strand.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/10 Polymerase Chain Reaction/04 The PCR cycle

cards.front: How many copies of a single DNA molecule are there after 20 perfect cycles?
cards.back: 2²⁰ = 1,048,576, over a million.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/10 Polymerase Chain Reaction/05 Amplification, doubling every cycle

cards.front: How many double-stranded molecules does the second cycle produce from one starting molecule?
cards.back: Four.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/10 Polymerase Chain Reaction/05 Amplification, doubling every cycle

cards.front: Why is the real increase less than ×2 per cycle in later cycles?
cards.back: Reagents such as primers and dNTPs run low and the polymerase loses activity, so not every molecule is copied.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/10 Polymerase Chain Reaction/05 Amplification, doubling every cycle

cards.front: Calculate Tm for CTTGCCCTACAGGCTTAGCC.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/10 Polymerase Chain Reaction/06 Primer design and melting temperature

cards.front: What annealing temperature would you use for a primer with Tm 64 °C?
cards.back: About 59 °C (Tm − 5 °C).
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/10 Polymerase Chain Reaction/06 Primer design and melting temperature

cards.front: Which way do the 3′ ends of the two primers point?
cards.back: Towards each other, across the region to be amplified.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/10 Polymerase Chain Reaction/06 Primer design and melting temperature

cards.front: Why does GC content raise Tm?
cards.back: G–C pairs have three hydrogen bonds, A–T pairs only two.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/10 Polymerase Chain Reaction/06 Primer design and melting temperature

cards.front: Give three uses of PCR from the lecture.
cards.back: Amplifying a gene for cloning (e.g. into an expression vector), amplifying DNA for sequencing (phylogenetics, diagnosis), and genetic fingerprinting (forensics, paternity testing).
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/10 Polymerase Chain Reaction/07 Uses of PCR

cards.front: Give one limitation of PCR.
cards.back: You need some sequence information to design primers; contamination with other DNA also causes false results.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/10 Polymerase Chain Reaction/07 Uses of PCR

cards.front: What enzyme lets PCR start from RNA?
cards.back: Reverse transcriptase, which makes a cDNA copy first.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/10 Polymerase Chain Reaction/08 RNA templates and real-time PCR

cards.front: What does real-time PCR measure?
cards.back: The amount of product after each cycle, from fluorescence, so the starting amount can be compared.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/10 Polymerase Chain Reaction/08 RNA templates and real-time PCR

cards.front: In real-time PCR, which sample's fluorescence rises earlier?
cards.back: The one with more starting template, e.g. the high gene expression sample.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/10 Polymerase Chain Reaction/08 RNA templates and real-time PCR

cards.front: What's the purpose of building a standard curve in the DNA concentration practical?
cards.back: To convert an absorbance reading into a DNA concentration, by measuring several samples of known concentration, plotting concentration against absorbance, and fitting a line through the points.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Practicals/01 DNA Concentration/01 Aim and setup (DNA Concentration)

cards.front: What do TRIS and EDTA each do in TE buffer?
cards.back: TRIS keeps the pH stable. EDTA binds the metal ions that DNA-degrading enzymes need as cofactors, so it protects the DNA from being broken down.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Practicals/01 DNA Concentration/01 Aim and setup (DNA Concentration)

cards.front: Why does tube 6 (buffer only, no DNA) get used to zero the spectrophotometer first?
cards.back: It contains no DNA, so its reading represents the baseline. The instrument gets zeroed against it before any of the actual DNA samples get measured.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Practicals/01 DNA Concentration/04 Measuring absorbance

cards.front: A tube with no DNA gives a slightly negative absorbance reading. Is that a problem?
cards.back: No. Every instrument has some inherent inaccuracy, so a small reading close to zero (within about ±0.1) is expected. Anything further off than that suggests an error in the solution or technique.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Practicals/01 DNA Concentration/04 Measuring absorbance

cards.front: What do you plot for the standard curve, and what do you do with the line?
cards.back: Concentration (or the volume of DNA standard added) on the x-axis against absorbance on the y-axis gives a straight line. Its equation, y = mx + c, converts a new absorbance reading into a concentration.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Practicals/01 DNA Concentration/05 Analysing the results

cards.front: What does an R² value close to 1 tell you?
cards.back: A strong, highly linear fit of the data to the line. Values close to 0 mean the line barely describes the data.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Practicals/01 DNA Concentration/05 Analysing the results

cards.front: What volume ranges do the P200 and P1000 pipettes cover?
cards.back: P200: 20 to 200 µL (small white or yellow tips). P1000: 200 to 1000 µL (larger white tips).
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Practicals/01 DNA Concentration/07 Pre-lab prep (DNA Concentration)

cards.front: Why press to the second stop when dispensing?
cards.back: The first stop expels most of the liquid and the second stop expels the last drops.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Practicals/01 DNA Concentration/07 Pre-lab prep (DNA Concentration)

cards.front: What is special about the sequence a restriction enzyme recognises?
cards.back: It is one specific short sequence (its recognition site), usually palindromic: read 5′ to 3′, it is identical on both strands.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Practicals/02 Restriction Mapping/01 Aim and background (Restriction Mapping)

cards.front: How many fragments do you get by cutting a circular plasmid at 1, 2 and 3 sites?
cards.back: One cut just opens the circle into a single linear fragment. Two cuts give 2 fragments and 3 cuts give 3.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Practicals/02 Restriction Mapping/01 Aim and background (Restriction Mapping)

cards.front: Which three enzymes are used in Practical 2, and how many different digests do they give?
cards.back: HindIII, PstI and PvuII, giving 7 digests: 3 single, 3 double and 1 triple.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Practicals/02 Restriction Mapping/02 Setting up the digest

cards.front: Why do smaller DNA fragments travel further through the gel?
cards.back: DNA's negatively charged backbone pulls it toward the positive electrode, and smaller fragments move further through the gel's mesh in the same time.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Practicals/02 Restriction Mapping/03 Running the gel

cards.front: What is the 1 kb ladder for?
cards.back: It is a set of fragments of known size run alongside the samples, so an unknown fragment's size can be estimated from how far it migrated.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Practicals/02 Restriction Mapping/03 Running the gel

cards.front: Why do gloves stay on when handling the gel?
cards.back: The gels contain ethidium bromide, which is a teratogen and a potential carcinogen.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Practicals/02 Restriction Mapping/03 Running the gel

cards.front: In the pABC123 worked example, why does each single-enzyme digest produce only one fragment?
cards.back: Because the plasmid is circular. Cutting a circular molecule once just opens it into a single linear fragment, rather than producing multiple pieces. Multiple fragments only appear once there are 2 or more cuts.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Practicals/02 Restriction Mapping/04 Building a restriction map from the data

cards.front: How do you work out the size of an unknown DNA fragment from a gel?
cards.back: Plot log₁₀(marker fragment size in bp) against distance migrated (mm) for the marker/ladder bands, producing a standard curve. Measure the unknown fragment's migration distance and read its size off that curve.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Practicals/02 Restriction Mapping/04 Building a restriction map from the data

cards.front: Why do two different arrangements (Option 1 and Option 2) both fit a double digest's fragment sizes equally well?
cards.back: A double digest only tells you the distances between two sites going each way round the circle, it doesn't tell you which direction each site sits in relative to a third site already placed. Both arrangements satisfy that same pair of distances until further data rules one out.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Practicals/02 Restriction Mapping/04 Building a restriction map from the data

cards.front: How do you decide which of two candidate restriction maps is actually correct?
cards.back: Compare the fragment sizes each candidate map predicts for the triple digest against the fragment sizes actually observed. Only the correct map's prediction matches the real result.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Practicals/02 Restriction Mapping/04 Building a restriction map from the data

cards.front: Why are transformed cells grown on ampicillin plates?
cards.back: pBR322 carries an ampicillin resistance gene (bla), so only cells that took up the plasmid survive.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Practicals/03 Transformation/01 Aim and background (Transformation)

cards.front: How is competency induced in the practical?
cards.back: Artificially, with calcium chloride. Cells sit on ice with the plasmid, then get a brief heat shock at 42°C that lets the plasmid cross into the cell.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Practicals/03 Transformation/01 Aim and background (Transformation)

cards.front: Why is there a 30 minute recovery step in LB broth at 37°C?
cards.back: It lets the ampicillin-resistance gene get expressed before the cells meet the antibiotic.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Practicals/03 Transformation/02 Transforming the cells

cards.front: What are the heat shock conditions?
cards.back: 42°C for precisely 50 seconds, then straight back onto ice for 2 minutes.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Practicals/03 Transformation/02 Transforming the cells

cards.front: Why does the transformation experiment include a control plate of untransformed cells on ampicillin?
cards.back: To confirm the bacteria weren't already ampicillin-resistant before transformation, so any growth on the actual transformation's ampicillin plate can be attributed to the plasmid.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Practicals/03 Transformation/03 Setting up the dilution series

cards.front: What is a colony-forming unit (CFU)?
cards.back: A single live bacterial cell capable of growing into one visible colony on an agar plate.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Practicals/03 Transformation/04 Calculating transformation efficiency

cards.front: What's the formula for calculating cells per mL from a dilution plate count?
cards.back: Cells per mL = colonies counted × 10^|dilution| × 10. The final × 10 is because 100 µL (0.1 mL) was spread on the plate.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Practicals/03 Transformation/04 Calculating transformation efficiency

cards.front: How do you calculate the frequency of transformation?
cards.back: Divide the number of transformed cells (CFU/mL) by the total number of cells (CFU/mL) used in the transformation.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Practicals/03 Transformation/04 Calculating transformation efficiency

cards.front: How should twenty five milligrams be written?
cards.back: 25 mg: value, space, then prefix and unit.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Professional Skills for Biosciences/Lectures/01 Measurements and Dilutions/01 Why units matter

cards.front: Name the seven SI base units.
cards.back: Metre (m), second (s), kilogram (kg), ampere (A), kelvin (K), mole (mol), candela (cd).
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Professional Skills for Biosciences/Lectures/01 Measurements and Dilutions/02 SI units

cards.front: Is the litre an SI unit?
cards.back: No, but it is accepted with SI: 1 L = 1 dm³ = 1/1000 m³.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Professional Skills for Biosciences/Lectures/01 Measurements and Dilutions/02 SI units

cards.front: Convert 5 nL to mL.
cards.back: 5 × 10⁻⁶ mL (nL and mL are 10⁶ apart).
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Professional Skills for Biosciences/Lectures/01 Measurements and Dilutions/04 Converting units

cards.front: Convert 2.5 μL to nL.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Professional Skills for Biosciences/Lectures/01 Measurements and Dilutions/04 Converting units

cards.front: Convert 150 m² to mm².
cards.back: 1 m² = 10⁶ mm², so 1.5 × 10⁸ mm².
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Professional Skills for Biosciences/Lectures/01 Measurements and Dilutions/04 Converting units

cards.front: A mitochondrion measures 0.8 mm in a picture at 10,000:1. What is its real size?
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Professional Skills for Biosciences/Lectures/01 Measurements and Dilutions/05 Scale and scale bars

cards.front: How is a 1 in 5 dilution made, and what does it do to 10⁵ bacteria mL⁻¹?
cards.back: 1 part culture + 4 parts medium. It gives 2 × 10⁴ bacteria mL⁻¹.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Professional Skills for Biosciences/Lectures/01 Measurements and Dilutions/06 Dilutions

cards.front: A 10⁸ cells mL⁻¹ culture goes through four 1 in 10 dilutions. What is the final concentration?
cards.back: 10⁴ cells mL⁻¹.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Professional Skills for Biosciences/Lectures/01 Measurements and Dilutions/07 Serial dilutions

cards.front: What does a 1 in 2 dilution of 10⁸ cells mL⁻¹ give?
cards.back: 5 × 10⁷ cells mL⁻¹ (equal volumes of culture and medium).
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Professional Skills for Biosciences/Lectures/01 Measurements and Dilutions/07 Serial dilutions

cards.front: Make V₂ the subject of C₁V₁ = C₂V₂.
cards.back: V₂ = C₁V₁ / C₂.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Professional Skills for Biosciences/Lectures/02 Maths for Biologists/01 Rearranging equations

cards.note: 01 Year 1/Professional Skills for Biosciences/Lectures/02 Maths for Biologists/01 Rearranging equations

cards.note: 01 Year 1/Professional Skills for Biosciences/Lectures/02 Maths for Biologists/02 Measurements, volumes and densities

cards.note: 01 Year 1/Professional Skills for Biosciences/Lectures/02 Maths for Biologists/06 Linear graphs

cards.front: What are the axes and intercepts of a Lineweaver-Burk plot?
cards.back: y = 1/v, x = 1/[S]; y intercept 1/Vmax, x intercept −1/Km.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Professional Skills for Biosciences/Lectures/02 Maths for Biologists/07 Non-linear graphs and enzyme kinetics

cards.front: Differentiate y = 3x², then integrate 3x².
cards.back: dy/dx = 6x. ∫3x² dx = x³ + C.
