cards.front: 5′ cap
cards.back: A G added to the 5′ end of eukaryotic mRNA through a 5′-5′ triphosphate link, then methylated.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/5′ cap

cards.front: A site
cards.back: The ribosome site that accepts the incoming aminoacyl-tRNA.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/A site

cards.front: AIDS
cards.back: The most advanced stage of HIV infection, taking 2 to 15 years to develop without treatment. The immune system can no longer fight off opportunistic infections.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/AIDS

cards.front: Activation energy
cards.back: The minimum energy a reactant molecule must have for a reaction to proceed, in kJ mol⁻¹.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Activation energy

cards.front: What does a catalyst do to the activation energy?
cards.back: Lowers it.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Activation energy

cards.front: Acute HIV infection
cards.back: The first stage of HIV infection: flu-like symptoms, a high viral load and destruction of CD4+ T-cells.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Acute HIV infection

cards.front: Addition reaction
cards.back: A reaction in which two molecules combine into one product containing all their atoms, across a C=C or C=O double bond: A + B → AB.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Addition reaction

cards.front: Which double bonds undergo addition?
cards.back: C=C in alkenes and C=O in carbonyls.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Addition reaction

cards.front: Agrobacterium tumefaciens
cards.back: A soil bacterium that causes crown gall disease by inserting part of its own DNA (the T-DNA from its Ti plasmid) into a plant's genome.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Agrobacterium tumefaciens

cards.front: Aldehyde
cards.back: A molecule with a carbonyl group at the end of the chain, such as pentanal.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Aldehyde

cards.front: Alkane
cards.back: A chain of carbon and hydrogen with only single bonds: saturated.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Alkane

cards.front: Alkene
cards.back: A hydrocarbon with a C=C double bond: unsaturated.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Alkene

cards.front: Alkyl group
cards.back: An alkane with one hydrogen removed so it can attach to another molecule, e.g. methyl –CH₃.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Alkyl group

cards.front: Alternative splicing
cards.back: Joining exons in different combinations so one gene makes several mRNAs and proteins.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Alternative splicing

cards.front: Amino group
cards.back: –NH₂. Found in every amino acid; amines are primary, secondary or tertiary.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Amino group

cards.front: Aminoacyl-tRNA
cards.back: A tRNA with its amino acid attached (a charged tRNA). It enters the ribosome at the A site.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Aminoacyl-tRNA

cards.front: Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase
cards.back: The enzyme that attaches an amino acid to its matching tRNAs (charging), using ATP. There is one for each of the 20 amino acids.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase

cards.front: Ampicillin resistance
cards.back: The bla gene on pBR322 lets cells grow on ampicillin, so growth on ampicillin plates selects for cells that took up the plasmid.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Ampicillin resistance

cards.front: Anion
cards.back: A negative ion, formed by gaining electrons.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Anion

cards.front: Annealing
cards.back: Cooling so that complementary single strands, such as primers and template, base-pair. In PCR it happens at 50–65 °C.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Annealing

cards.front: Anticodon
cards.back: The three bases on a tRNA that pair with a codon on the mRNA, e.g. UAC pairs with AUG.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Anticodon

cards.front: Antioxidant
cards.back: A molecule, such as vitamin C or E, that quenches free radicals by forming much less reactive radicals.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Antioxidant

cards.front: Give two antioxidants.
cards.back: Vitamin C and vitamin E.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Antioxidant

cards.front: Antiparallel
cards.back: The two strands of the double helix run in opposite directions: one 5' to 3', the other 3' to 5'.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Antiparallel

cards.front: Aryl group
cards.back: In the lecture: a group from a cyclic alkane. In most textbooks: an aromatic ring such as phenyl.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Aryl group

cards.front: B-DNA
cards.back: The predominant form of DNA in cells. A-DNA and Z-DNA also occur, with different helical structures.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/B-DNA

cards.front: Bacteria
cards.back: Single-celled prokaryotes: simple cells with no nucleus or membrane-bound organelles. Most are harmless and relatively few cause disease.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Bacteria

cards.front: Bacteriophage
cards.back: A virus that infects bacteria or archaea. Crick used phage T4 to show the genetic code is a triplet code.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Bacteriophage

cards.front: Basal transcription complex
cards.back: RNA Pol II plus TBP and its associated factors assembled on a eukaryotic promoter: the core machinery needed to start transcription.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Basal transcription complex

cards.front: Bidirectional replication
cards.back: Replication proceeds in both directions away from each origin, with a fork moving each way.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Bidirectional replication

cards.front: Biomedicine
cards.back: The study of the molecular and cellular basis of human disease, and how that knowledge is translated into diagnosis, monitoring, treatment and prevention.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Biomedicine

cards.front: Blue-white screening
cards.back: Spotting recombinant colonies on X-gal plates: an insert disrupts lacZ so those colonies stay white, while colonies without an insert turn blue.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Blue-white screening

cards.front: Blunt ends
cards.back: DNA ends with no overhang, made when a restriction enzyme cuts both strands at the same point, e.g. AluI.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Blunt ends

cards.front: Bond energy
cards.back: The energy needed to break one mole of a given bond, e.g. C–H 412 kJ mol⁻¹. Breaking bonds needs energy; forming them releases it.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Bond energy

cards.front: Is energy released when a bond forms or breaks?
cards.back: When it forms.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Bond energy

cards.front: CAP
cards.back: Catabolite activator protein: with cAMP bound, it binds next to the lac promoter and strongly activates transcription when glucose is low.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/CAP

cards.front: CD4
cards.back: The surface receptor on immune cells (T-cells, macrophages and monocytes) that HIV uses to infect them.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/CD4

cards.front: Carbonyl group
cards.back: C=O. At the end of a chain it makes an aldehyde, in the middle a ketone.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Carbonyl group

cards.front: Carboxyl group
cards.back: –COOH, which makes carboxylic acids. Found in every amino acid and fatty acid.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Carboxyl group

cards.front: Catalyst
cards.back: A substance that speeds up a reaction by giving a lower-activation-energy route, without being used up and without changing K.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Catalyst

cards.front: What does a catalyst not change?
cards.back: ΔG, K or the position of equilibrium; only the rate.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Catalyst

cards.front: Cation
cards.back: A positive ion, formed by losing electrons.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Cation

cards.front: Cell-free system
cards.back: Protein synthesis in a test tube: an RNA template, tRNAs carrying amino acids, ribosomes and an energy source (GTP), used to crack the genetic code.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Cell-free system

cards.front: Central dogma
cards.back: Crick's 1970 statement that sequence information flows from DNA to RNA to protein and cannot be transferred back from protein to protein or nucleic acid. Often put as 'DNA makes RNA and RNA makes protein'.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Central dogma

cards.front: Chargaff's rule
cards.back: In DNA the amount of A equals T and the amount of G equals C, whatever the species, even though the overall A+T versus G+C ratio varies widely between species.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Chargaff's rule

cards.front: Chromatin remodelling
cards.back: Loosening chromatin so the promoter is exposed, done by complexes such as SWI-SNF. Needed to activate eukaryotic transcription.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Chromatin remodelling

cards.front: Chromosome theory of inheritance
cards.back: Sutton and Boveri's 1902 proposal that chromosome behaviour during meiosis explains the patterns of inheritance Mendel observed.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Chromosome theory of inheritance

cards.front: Chronic HIV infection
cards.back: The long stage in which HIV multiplies at low levels with no symptoms, until the immune system is eventually overwhelmed.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Chronic HIV infection

cards.front: Cloning vector
cards.back: A DNA molecule, usually a plasmid, that accepts a DNA fragment and replicates it inside a host cell.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Cloning vector

cards.front: Coding strand
cards.back: The DNA strand with the same sequence as the mRNA (T in place of U). It is not read during transcription.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Coding strand

cards.front: Codon
cards.back: Three consecutive mRNA nucleotides that specify one amino acid or a stop signal. There are 64 codons.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Codon

cards.front: Colony-forming unit
cards.back: A single live cell that grows into one visible colony. Counting colonies gives the number of live cells per mL.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Colony-forming unit

cards.front: Commaless
cards.back: Codons are read one after the other with no gaps or spacer bases between them.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Commaless

cards.front: Communicable disease
cards.back: An infectious disease that spreads from person to person, such as influenza or measles.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Communicable disease

cards.front: Competence
cards.back: The physiological state a bacterial cell needs to take up foreign DNA. In the lab it is induced with calcium chloride and a heat shock.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Competence

cards.front: Complementary base pairing
cards.back: A pairs with T (2 hydrogen bonds) and G pairs with C (3 hydrogen bonds), so each strand specifies the sequence of its partner.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Complementary base pairing

cards.front: Condensation reaction
cards.back: A reaction joining two molecules with the loss of water. It makes glycosidic, ester and peptide bonds; hydrolysis reverses it.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Condensation reaction

cards.front: Consensus sequence
cards.back: The most common base at each position across many versions of a sequence, such as TATAAT for the −10 box.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Consensus sequence

cards.front: Constitutive expression
cards.back: A gene that is always switched on, for example lac genes in a mutant whose repressor cannot bind the operator.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Constitutive expression

cards.front: Coupled reaction
cards.back: Driving an endergonic reaction with an exergonic one so the total ΔG is negative, e.g. hexokinase: ΔG3 = ΔG1 + ΔG2 < 0.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Coupled reaction

cards.front: Give an example of coupling.
cards.back: Hexokinase couples ATP hydrolysis to phosphorylating glucose.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Coupled reaction

cards.front: Covalent bond
cards.back: A bond where two atoms share a pair of electrons. A double bond shares two pairs, a triple bond three.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Covalent bond

cards.front: DNA
cards.back: The molecule that stores genetic information. A double helix of two antiparallel strands, built from nucleotides and held together by base pairing.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/DNA

cards.front: DNA gyrase
cards.back: A topoisomerase that removes the supercoiling caused by unwinding the helix ahead of the fork.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/DNA gyrase

cards.front: DNA ligase
cards.back: Seals nicks in the DNA backbone by forming phosphodiester bonds. It joins Okazaki fragments in replication, and joins an insert to a vector in cloning.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/DNA ligase

cards.front: DNA polymerase
cards.back: The enzyme that builds new DNA by adding nucleotides to a free 3' end, proofreading as it goes.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/DNA polymerase

cards.front: DNA polymerase I
cards.back: Removes the RNA primers and replaces them with DNA.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/DNA polymerase I

cards.front: DNA polymerase III
cards.back: The main replication enzyme in E. coli. It does most of the actual DNA synthesis.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/DNA polymerase III

cards.front: Dative bond
cards.back: A covalent bond where both shared electrons come from one atom's lone pair, as in NH₄⁺. Also called a coordinate bond.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Dative bond

cards.front: Denaturation
cards.back: Separating the two strands of DNA by breaking the hydrogen bonds between bases (using heat or chemicals), without breaking the covalent backbone.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Denaturation

cards.front: Deoxyribose
cards.back: The sugar in DNA. It has just an H, with no OH, on its 2' carbon.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Deoxyribose

cards.front: Dilution factor
cards.back: How much a solution is diluted: 1 part in 10 total is a dilution factor of 10 (written 10⁻¹).
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Dilution factor

cards.front: Directionality
cards.back: Every nucleic acid strand has a free 5' end (phosphate) and a free 3' end (hydroxyl). Synthesis, transcription and translation all run 5' to 3'.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Directionality

cards.front: Disaccharide
cards.back: Two monosaccharides joined by a glycosidic bond, such as lactose, maltose or sucrose.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Disaccharide

cards.front: Dissociation constant
cards.back: The equilibrium constant for a complex falling apart, PL ⇌ P + L: Kd = [P][L] / [PL]. Small Kd means strong binding.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Dissociation constant

cards.front: Does a large Kd mean strong or weak binding?
cards.back: Weak binding.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Dissociation constant

cards.front: Disulfide bridge
cards.back: An S–S bond between two cysteines that holds parts of a folded protein together.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Disulfide bridge

cards.front: Dynamic equilibrium
cards.back: The state where forward and back reactions continue at equal rates, so concentrations no longer change (d[X]/dt = 0).
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Dynamic equilibrium

cards.front: Do reactions stop at equilibrium?
cards.back: No. Both directions continue at equal rates.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Dynamic equilibrium

cards.front: E site
cards.back: The ribosome site holding the free, uncharged tRNA before it leaves.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/E site

cards.front: Electron configuration
cards.back: How an atom's electrons fill its orbitals, e.g. carbon 1s² 2s² 2p².
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Electron configuration

cards.front: Electronegativity
cards.back: An atom's ability to pull the electrons of a covalent bond towards itself. Fluorine is highest; it rises across a period and falls down a group.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Electronegativity

cards.front: Electrophile
cards.back: An electron-deficient species with an empty valence orbital that accepts an electron pair, e.g. H⁺ or a δ+ carbon.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Electrophile

cards.front: What must an electrophile have?
cards.back: An empty valence orbital.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Electrophile

cards.front: Elimination
cards.back: Reduction to zero (or a very low target rate) of new cases within a defined area through deliberate effort, with continued measures still needed to stop transmission re-establishing. Example: measles.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Elimination

cards.front: Elimination reaction
cards.back: A reaction in which a molecule loses atoms from neighbouring positions, usually forming a double bond: AX–XB → X=X + A–B.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Elimination reaction

cards.front: What usually forms in an elimination?
cards.back: A double bond.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Elimination reaction

cards.front: Elongation factor
cards.back: GTP-using proteins that drive elongation: EF-Tu brings charged tRNAs to the A site, EF-G moves the ribosome along the mRNA.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Elongation factor

cards.front: What does EF-Tu do?
cards.back: Delivers charged tRNAs to the A site, checking the codon-anticodon match.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Elongation factor

cards.front: Endemic
cards.back: The amount of a disease that is usually present in a community.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Endemic

cards.front: Endergonic reaction
cards.back: A reaction with positive ΔG that needs an input of energy and is not spontaneous.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Endergonic reaction

cards.front: How can a cell make an endergonic reaction happen?
cards.back: Couple it to a strongly exergonic one, such as ATP hydrolysis.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Endergonic reaction

cards.front: Endothermic reaction
cards.back: A reaction with positive ΔH, in which heat flows from the surroundings into the system.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Endothermic reaction

cards.front: What is the sign of ΔH for an endothermic reaction?
cards.back: Positive.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Endothermic reaction

cards.front: Enhancer
cards.back: A DNA sequence bound by transcription factors that increases transcription from a promoter.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Enhancer

cards.front: Enthalpy
cards.back: The heat content of a system. Its change, ΔH (J mol⁻¹), is the energy change of a reaction. Negative ΔH is exothermic, positive is endothermic.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Enthalpy

cards.front: What does a negative ΔH mean?
cards.back: The reaction is exothermic, releasing heat to the surroundings.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Enthalpy

cards.front: Entropy
cards.back: A measure of how spread out energy is in a system (energetic disorder), units J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Solid < liquid < gas.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Entropy

cards.front: What must the total entropy change be for a spontaneous reaction?
cards.back: Greater than zero.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Entropy

cards.front: Epidemic
cards.back: The same as an outbreak: an increase, often sudden, in cases above what is normally expected for that population and area.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Epidemic

cards.front: Equilibrium constant
cards.back: The ratio of product to reactant concentrations at equilibrium, each raised to its stoichiometric coefficient: Kc = [C]ᶜ[D]ᵈ / [A]ᵃ[B]ᵇ.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Equilibrium constant

cards.front: What does K > 10² tell you?
cards.back: Equilibrium lies to the right; products dominate.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Equilibrium constant

cards.front: Eradication
cards.back: Complete, permanent, worldwide reduction to zero new cases through deliberate effort, with no further control measures needed. Example: smallpox.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Eradication

cards.front: Ester
cards.back: The link formed when a carboxyl group joins a hydroxyl group, losing water. Joins fatty acids to glycerol.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Ester

cards.front: Exergonic reaction
cards.back: A reaction with negative ΔG that releases free energy and can be spontaneous.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Exergonic reaction

cards.front: What is the sign of ΔG for an exergonic reaction?
cards.back: Negative.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Exergonic reaction

cards.front: Exothermic reaction
cards.back: A reaction with negative ΔH, in which heat flows from the system to the surroundings.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Exothermic reaction

cards.front: Which way does heat flow in an exothermic reaction?
cards.back: From the system to the surroundings.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Exothermic reaction

cards.front: Fatty acid
cards.back: A long hydrocarbon chain with a carboxyl group at one end.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Fatty acid

cards.front: Fidelity
cards.back: How accurately a DNA polymerase copies its template. Higher-fidelity enzymes are more expensive and slower.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Fidelity

cards.front: When would you choose a high-fidelity polymerase?
cards.back: When every base matters, e.g. cloning a gene to express it.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Fidelity

cards.front: Frameshift mutation
cards.back: An insertion or deletion that shifts the reading frame so every following codon is misread. In phage T4 rII, losing or adding one or two bases abolished function but three often did not, showing the code is read in triplets.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Frameshift mutation

cards.front: Free radical
cards.back: A species with an unpaired electron, shown by a dot (Cl•). Highly reactive and unstable.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Free radical

cards.front: Name the three stages of a free radical reaction.
cards.back: Initiation, propagation and termination.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Free radical

cards.front: Functional group
cards.back: A group of atoms on a carbon chain that gives the molecule its properties, such as –OH or –COOH.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Functional group

cards.front: Fungi
cards.back: A very diverse group (moulds, mushrooms, yeasts) found in almost any habitat. Most are harmless to humans, and a few cause disease, especially in immune-compromised people.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Fungi

cards.front: Gel electrophoresis
cards.back: Separating DNA fragments by size. DNA's negatively charged backbone pulls it toward the positive electrode through the gel, and smaller fragments move further.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Gel electrophoresis

cards.front: Genetic vaccine approach
cards.back: DNA and mRNA vaccines: a single viral gene is injected and the host's own cells make the immunogenic protein.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Genetic vaccine approach

cards.front: Gibberellin 3β-hydroxylase
cards.back: The enzyme encoded by the Le gene. It helps make gibberellin, the plant hormone that promotes stem growth. In the dwarf mutant one amino acid swap (A229T) cripples it.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Gibberellin 3β-hydroxylase

cards.front: Gibbs free energy
cards.back: The energy free to do work. ΔG = ΔH − TΔS; a reaction can be spontaneous when ΔG is negative.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Gibbs free energy

cards.front: Write the equation for ΔG.
cards.back: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Gibbs free energy

cards.front: Glycosidic bond
cards.back: The C–O–C link joining two sugars, made by a condensation reaction.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Glycosidic bond

cards.front: Gradient
cards.back: The steepness of a straight line: change in y ÷ change in x, the m in y = mx + c.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Gradient

cards.front: Gram-negative bacteria
cards.back: Bacteria with a thinner peptidoglycan layer plus an outer membrane. They lose the crystal violet stain and look pink after the safranin counterstain.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Gram-negative bacteria

cards.front: Gram-positive bacteria
cards.back: Bacteria with several layers of peptidoglycan. They keep the crystal violet stain and look purple.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Gram-positive bacteria

cards.front: HAART
cards.back: Highly active anti-retroviral therapy: three or more antiretroviral drugs that suppress HIV to undetectable levels. It does not cure HIV, but lets the immune system recover.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/HAART

cards.front: Heat shock
cards.back: A brief jump to 42 degrees C after the cells and DNA have sat on ice. It helps the plasmid cross into the cell.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Heat shock

cards.front: Helicase
cards.back: The enzyme (DnaB in E. coli) that unwinds the double helix at the fork.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Helicase

cards.front: Henderson-Hasselbalch equation
cards.back: pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]): links pH to the ratio of base to acid in a buffer.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Henderson-Hasselbalch equation

cards.front: Heredity
cards.back: The passing of physical or mental characteristics from one generation to the next.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Heredity

cards.front: Hess's law
cards.back: The enthalpy change of a reaction is the same whatever route is taken, so ΔH°reaction = ΣΔHf°(products) − ΣΔHf°(reactants).
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Hess's law

cards.front: What does Hess's law let you calculate?
cards.back: ΔH of a reaction from standard enthalpies of formation, or from any other route.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Hess's law

cards.front: Heterolytic fission
cards.back: Bond breaking in which one atom keeps both electrons of the bond, forming a negative and a positive ion.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Heterolytic fission

cards.front: In heterolytic fission, which atom usually keeps the electron pair?
cards.back: The more electronegative one.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Heterolytic fission

cards.front: Homolytic fission
cards.back: Bond breaking in which the shared electron pair splits, one electron to each atom, forming two free radicals.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Homolytic fission

cards.front: What does homolytic fission produce?
cards.back: Two free radicals.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Homolytic fission

cards.front: Hybridisation
cards.back: Mixing an atom's s and p orbitals into equal hybrid orbitals before bonding: sp (180°), sp² (120°) or sp³ (109.5°).
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Hybridisation

cards.front: Hydration reaction
cards.back: An addition reaction in which water (H and OH) adds across a double bond, e.g. an aldehyde forming a hydrate. The molecule stays intact.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Hydration reaction

cards.front: How does hydration differ from hydrolysis?
cards.back: Hydration adds water across a double bond without splitting the molecule; hydrolysis splits a molecule.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Hydration reaction

cards.front: Hydrogen bond
cards.back: A weak attraction between a δ+ hydrogen and a lone pair on a nearby O or N. Holds water molecules together and DNA's two strands.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Hydrogen bond

cards.front: Hydrolysis
cards.back: Breaking a bond by adding water, which is split between the two fragments. The reverse of a condensation reaction.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Hydrolysis

cards.front: Which reaction breaks proteins into amino acids?
cards.back: Hydrolysis of the peptide bonds.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Hydrolysis

cards.front: Hydroxyl group
cards.back: –OH, which makes alcohols and makes molecules more polar.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Hydroxyl group

cards.front: Hyperchromic effect
cards.back: The rise in UV absorbance at 260 nm as DNA denatures, because unstacked single-stranded bases absorb more UV than stacked double-stranded ones.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Hyperchromic effect

cards.front: Infectious disease
cards.back: Disease caused by a pathogenic microorganism: bacteria, viruses, fungi or parasites. Examples: tetanus, influenza, measles.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Infectious disease

cards.front: Initiation factor
cards.back: Proteins (IF1, IF2, IF3 in bacteria) that assemble the ribosome, mRNA and initiator tRNA at the start codon.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Initiation factor

cards.front: What does IF2 do?
cards.back: Brings fMet-tRNA to the 30S-mRNA complex so it pairs with AUG in the P site.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Initiation factor

cards.front: Internal energy
cards.back: The total energy of a system, which can be transferred as work (w) or heat (q): U = w + q.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Internal energy

cards.front: Write the equation for internal energy.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Internal energy

cards.front: Ionic bond
cards.back: A bond formed when one atom transfers electrons to another, so the resulting cation and anion attract.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Ionic bond

cards.front: Isotope
cards.back: Atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but a different number of neutrons, such as ¹⁴N and ¹⁵N.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Isotope

cards.front: Ketone
cards.back: A molecule with a carbonyl group in the middle of the chain, such as pentan-3-one.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Ketone

cards.front: Kinetic energy
cards.back: The energy of motion, E = ½mv².
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Kinetic energy

cards.front: What two quantities set kinetic energy?
cards.back: Mass and speed: E = ½mv².
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Kinetic energy

cards.front: Lagging strand
cards.back: The new strand made discontinuously, as short Okazaki fragments running against the direction of the fork, because DNA polymerase only builds 5' to 3'.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Lagging strand

cards.front: Latent infection
cards.back: A viral infection in which viral DNA sits in the host cell without replicating.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Latent infection

cards.front: Le Chatelier's principle
cards.back: When a system at equilibrium is disturbed, its composition adjusts to minimise the effect of the disturbance.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Le Chatelier's principle

cards.front: What happens to K when you add more reactant?
cards.back: Nothing. The equilibrium shifts forward, but K stays the same.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Le Chatelier's principle

cards.front: Leading strand
cards.back: The new strand made continuously, in the same direction the replication fork moves.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Leading strand

cards.front: Leaving group
cards.back: The atom or group that departs with the bonding electron pair in a substitution or elimination, e.g. Br⁻. The best leaving groups are highly electronegative.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Leaving group

cards.front: What is the leaving group when OH⁻ reacts with bromoethane?
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Leaving group

cards.front: Lineweaver-Burk plot
cards.back: 1/v against 1/[S]: a straight-line version of the Michaelis-Menten equation, with y intercept 1/Vmax and x intercept −1/Km.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Lineweaver-Burk plot

cards.front: Logarithm
cards.back: The power a base must be raised to: log₁₀(1000) = 3. Biology uses base 10 and the natural log, ln.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Logarithm

cards.front: Lone pair
cards.back: A pair of valence electrons not used in bonding. Lone pairs repel more strongly than bonds.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Lone pair

cards.front: Lytic infection
cards.back: A viral infection in which the virus replicates and destroys the host cell, releasing new virus.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Lytic infection

cards.front: Major groove
cards.back: The wider groove of the double helix. It exposes more of each base pair's chemical detail, so sequence-reading proteins such as transcription factors typically bind there.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Major groove

cards.front: Meiosis
cards.back: The cell division that produces gametes. Chromosome behaviour during meiosis explains Mendel's inheritance patterns.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Meiosis

cards.front: Melting temperature
cards.back: The temperature at which half of a DNA sample has denatured. More G and C gives a higher value, because G to C pairs have 3 hydrogen bonds against 2 for A to T.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Melting temperature

cards.front: Messenger RNA
cards.back: The RNA copy of a gene that carries its sequence to the ribosome, where it is read three bases at a time.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Messenger RNA

cards.front: Michaelis-Menten equation
cards.back: v = Vmax[S] / (Km + [S]): how an enzyme's reaction rate depends on substrate concentration.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Michaelis-Menten equation

cards.front: Molar mass
cards.back: The mass of one mole of a substance, in g mol⁻¹. Moles = mass ÷ molar mass.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Molar mass

cards.front: Molarity
cards.back: Concentration in moles per litre (mol L⁻¹, written M).
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Molarity

cards.front: Molecular hybridization
cards.back: Complementary single strands from different sources re-annealing and base-pairing with each other.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Molecular hybridization

cards.front: Monosaccharide
cards.back: A single sugar unit, such as glucose, fructose or galactose.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Monosaccharide

cards.front: Multiple cloning site
cards.back: A short region of a vector packed with unique restriction sites where DNA can be inserted. In pUC18 it sits inside lacZ.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Multiple cloning site

cards.front: N-formylmethionine
cards.back: A modified methionine (fMet) used as the first amino acid of polypeptide chains in bacteria.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/N-formylmethionine

cards.front: Noble gas
cards.back: Group 8 (0 or 18) elements with full valence shells, so they are very unreactive.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Noble gas

cards.front: Non-overlapping code
cards.back: Each nucleotide belongs to only one codon, so codons never share bases.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Non-overlapping code

cards.front: Nucleoid
cards.back: The single loop of DNA in a bacterial cell's cytoplasm that holds its genetic information.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Nucleoid

cards.front: Nucleophile
cards.back: An electron-rich species with a lone pair it can donate to form a covalent bond, e.g. OH⁻, H₂O, Cl⁻.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Nucleophile

cards.front: What does a nucleophile donate?
cards.back: An electron pair.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Nucleophile

cards.front: Nucleoside
cards.back: A base joined to a sugar, with no phosphate. Add phosphate groups and it becomes a nucleotide.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Nucleoside

cards.front: Nucleotide
cards.back: The building block of DNA and RNA: a 5-carbon sugar, a phosphate group and a nitrogenous base.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Nucleotide

cards.front: Obligate intracellular parasite
cards.back: An organism that can only replicate inside a host cell. Viruses are one: they rely on the host for energy, metabolic intermediates and protein synthesis.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Obligate intracellular parasite

cards.front: Okazaki fragments
cards.back: The short pieces in which the lagging strand is made, roughly 1,000 to 2,000 nucleotides long in bacteria and 150 to 200 in eukaryotes. Ligase joins them up.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Okazaki fragments

cards.front: Oligonucleotide
cards.back: A short, single-stranded, chemically synthesised piece of DNA or RNA, e.g. a PCR primer of about 20 nucleotides.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Oligonucleotide

cards.front: Operator
cards.back: The DNA site next to a promoter where a repressor binds to block RNA polymerase.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Operator

cards.front: Operon
cards.back: A unit of linked genes under the control of a single promoter, such as the lac operon.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Operon

cards.front: Outbreak
cards.back: A sudden increase in cases of a disease above what is normally expected in that population and area.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Outbreak

cards.front: P site
cards.back: The ribosome site holding the peptidyl-tRNA, the tRNA attached to the growing chain. The initiator fMet-tRNA starts here.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/P site

cards.front: Palindromic
cards.back: Reads the same 5' to 3' on both strands. Restriction enzyme recognition sites are usually palindromic.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Palindromic

cards.front: Pandemic
cards.back: An epidemic that has spread over multiple countries or continents, usually affecting a large number of people.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Pandemic

cards.front: Parasitism
cards.back: A relationship in which a parasite lives off a host, taking essential nutrients from it. It usually causes disease in the host.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Parasitism

cards.front: Peptide bond
cards.back: The bond joining amino acids: the carboxyl group of one joins the amino group of the next, losing water.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Peptide bond

cards.front: Peptidoglycan
cards.back: The main component of the bacterial cell wall. It protects against osmotic lysis and gives the cell its shape.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Peptidoglycan

cards.front: Peptidyl transferase
cards.back: The catalytic activity of the large ribosomal subunit (23S rRNA) that forms each peptide bond.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Peptidyl transferase

cards.front: Persistent infection
cards.back: A viral infection in which the virus replicates and is released by budding, without destroying the host cell.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Persistent infection

cards.front: Phosphodiester bond
cards.back: The bond linking nucleotides together, between the 5' carbon of one sugar and the 3' carbon of the next.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Phosphodiester bond

cards.front: Plasmid
cards.back: An extra circle of DNA carried by some bacteria, separate from the main chromosome.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Plasmid

cards.front: Polar bond
cards.back: A covalent bond where one atom pulls the electrons harder, giving δ+ and δ− ends, such as O–H.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Polar bond

cards.front: Poly-A tail
cards.back: 100 to 200 A residues added by poly-A polymerase after the 3′ end is cut downstream of AAUAAA.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Poly-A tail

cards.front: Polymerase chain reaction
cards.back: An in vitro method that amplifies a chosen DNA sequence through repeated cycles of denaturation, primer annealing and extension by a thermostable DNA polymerase.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Polymerase chain reaction

cards.front: Polynucleotide
cards.back: A long chain of linked nucleotides. This is what DNA and RNA strands actually are.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Polynucleotide

cards.front: Polynucleotide phosphorylase
cards.back: An enzyme that joins ribonucleoside diphosphates into RNA without needing a DNA template. Nirenberg and Matthaei used it to make synthetic RNAs such as poly-U.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Polynucleotide phosphorylase

cards.front: Polyribosome
cards.back: One mRNA being translated by several ribosomes at the same time.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Polyribosome

cards.front: Potential energy
cards.back: Stored energy due to position (gravitational, Ep = mgh) or held in chemical bonds (chemical potential energy).
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Potential energy

cards.front: Which type of potential energy matters most in biology?
cards.back: Chemical potential energy, stored in bonds.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Potential energy

cards.front: Primary transcript
cards.back: The first RNA copy of a eukaryotic gene, containing exons and introns, before capping, tailing and splicing.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Primary transcript

cards.front: Primase
cards.back: An RNA polymerase that makes the short RNA primer DNA polymerase needs in order to start.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Primase

cards.front: Primer
cards.back: A short nucleic acid strand that gives DNA polymerase a free 3′ end to extend. In replication it is RNA (10 to 12 nucleotides in E. coli), made by primase. In PCR it is a synthetic DNA oligonucleotide of about 20 nucleotides.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Primer

cards.front: Promoter
cards.back: The DNA sequence upstream of a gene where RNA polymerase binds and transcription starts. In E. coli it has −35 (TTGACA) and −10 (TATAAT) boxes.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Promoter

cards.front: Purines
cards.back: The two bases with two rings: adenine and guanine.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Purines

cards.front: Pyrimidines
cards.back: The bases with one ring: cytosine, thymine (DNA only) and uracil (RNA only).
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Pyrimidines

cards.front: Pyrrolysine
cards.back: Pyl, O: like lysine with an extra pyrroline group. In some species UAG, normally a stop codon, encodes it. Found in methanogenic archaea and Desulfitobacterium hafniense.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Pyrrolysine

cards.front: RNA polymerase
cards.back: The enzyme that makes an RNA copy of DNA by reading the template strand. E. coli's has 2 α, β, β′ and σ subunits; eukaryotes use RNA Pol II for mRNA.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/RNA polymerase

cards.front: Rate-limiting step
cards.back: The step with the highest-energy transition state, which sets the rate of the overall reaction.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Rate-limiting step

cards.front: What sets the rate of a multi-step reaction?
cards.back: The step with the highest-energy transition state.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Rate-limiting step

cards.front: Reaction intermediate
cards.back: A species formed in one step of a reaction and used up in a later step. It sits in an energy dip between two transition states.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Reaction intermediate

cards.front: Where does an intermediate sit on an energy profile?
cards.back: In a dip between two transition states.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Reaction intermediate

cards.front: Reaction mechanism
cards.back: The step-by-step description of which bonds break and form, and how electrons move, as reactants become products.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Reaction mechanism

cards.front: What does a mechanism add to a reaction scheme?
cards.back: How the change happens: bond breaking and forming, electron movement and the number of steps.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Reaction mechanism

cards.front: Reaction quotient
cards.back: The same ratio as K but for any moment, not only at equilibrium. At equilibrium Q = K.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Reaction quotient

cards.front: When does Q equal K?
cards.back: At equilibrium.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Reaction quotient

cards.front: Reaction rate
cards.back: How fast a reaction goes: the change measured divided by the change in time. Found by experiment, not from ΔG.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Reaction rate

cards.front: Can ΔG predict reaction rate?
cards.back: No; rates are measured experimentally.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Reaction rate

cards.front: Reading frame
cards.back: The way an mRNA is divided into successive codons, set by the start codon.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Reading frame

cards.front: Real-time PCR
cards.back: PCR in which the product is measured by fluorescence after every cycle, so the starting amount of template can be compared.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Real-time PCR

cards.front: Recognition site
cards.back: The specific short DNA sequence a restriction enzyme cuts at.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Recognition site

cards.front: Recombinant DNA
cards.back: DNA artificially combined from two different sources, for example a bacterial plasmid backbone plus a gene from another organism.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Recombinant DNA

cards.front: Redundancy
cards.back: 61 codons encode 20 amino acids, so most amino acids have more than one codon. Synonymous codons usually differ at the third base.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Redundancy

cards.front: Release factor
cards.back: A protein that binds a stop codon in the A site and triggers release of the finished polypeptide. RF1: UAA, UAG. RF2: UAA, UGA.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Release factor

cards.front: Which stop codons does RF2 recognise?
cards.back: UAA and UGA.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Release factor

cards.front: Repeating copolymer
cards.back: A synthetic RNA built from a short repeated sequence, such as UCUCUC. Khorana used them to assign codons: repeating UC gives UCU and CUC, coding leucine and serine.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Repeating copolymer

cards.front: Replication fork
cards.back: The Y-shaped point where the helix is actively unwound and copied.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Replication fork

cards.front: Repressor
cards.back: A protein that blocks transcription by binding an operator. The lac repressor (from lacI) lets go when it binds lactose.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Repressor

cards.front: Restriction enzyme
cards.back: An enzyme that cuts double-stranded DNA only at one specific short sequence, its recognition site.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Restriction enzyme

cards.front: Restriction map
cards.back: A map of the number, order and distances between restriction sites in a DNA molecule, worked out from single and double digests on a gel.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Restriction map

cards.front: What gel lanes are used to build a restriction map?
cards.back: Uncut DNA, each single digest, and the double digest, next to size markers.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Restriction map

cards.front: Reverse transcription PCR
cards.back: PCR that starts from RNA: reverse transcriptase first copies the RNA into cDNA, which is then amplified.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Reverse transcription PCR

cards.front: Reversible reaction
cards.back: A reaction that can go both ways, written with ⇌: A + B ⇌ C + D.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Reversible reaction

cards.front: How is a reversible reaction written?
cards.back: With a double arrow, ⇌.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Reversible reaction

cards.front: Ribose
cards.back: The sugar in RNA. It has an OH group on its 2' carbon.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Ribose

cards.front: Ribosome
cards.back: The site of translation, where mRNA codons are matched to tRNAs and amino acids are joined into a polypeptide.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Ribosome

cards.front: Ribozyme
cards.back: An RNA molecule with catalytic activity. The ribosome is one, because its 23S rRNA forms peptide bonds.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Ribozyme

cards.front: SI unit
cards.back: The international system of units: metre, second, kilogram, ampere, kelvin, mole and candela, plus units built from them.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/SI unit

cards.front: Scale bar
cards.back: A line on an image labelled with the real length it represents.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Scale bar

cards.front: Segregation
cards.back: The separation of paired chromosomes, and the gene versions they carry, into different gametes during meiosis. It is the physical reason behind Mendel's 3:1 ratio.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Segregation

cards.front: Selectable marker
cards.back: A vector gene, often antibiotic resistance, that lets you pick out host cells that took up the vector.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Selectable marker

cards.front: Selenocysteine
cards.back: Sec, U: like cysteine but with selenium in place of sulphur. In some proteins in some species UGA, normally a stop codon, encodes it. Found in fewer than 100 human proteins.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Selenocysteine

cards.front: Semi-discontinuous
cards.back: How double-stranded DNA is replicated: one strand is made continuously (leading) and the other discontinuously (lagging).
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Semi-discontinuous

cards.front: Semiconservative replication
cards.back: DNA replication in which each daughter molecule has one original (parental) strand and one newly made strand. Shown by Meselson and Stahl in 1958.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Semiconservative replication

cards.front: Serial dilution
cards.back: Diluting by the same factor again and again, usually 1 mL into 9 mL each time for a series of 10-fold dilutions.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Serial dilution

cards.front: Shine-Dalgarno sequence
cards.back: The ribosome binding site on bacterial mRNA (AGGAGG), a few bases before the AUG, which pairs with the 16S rRNA.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Shine-Dalgarno sequence

cards.front: Sigma factor
cards.back: The RNA polymerase subunit (σ) that recognises the −10 and −35 promoter boxes. Different sigma factors switch on different sets of genes.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Sigma factor

cards.front: Spliceosome
cards.back: The large RNA-protein complex (60S in mammals) that removes introns, using snRNPs that base pair with intron sequences.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Spliceosome

cards.front: Splicing
cards.back: Removing introns from a primary transcript and joining the exons, done by the spliceosome.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Splicing

cards.front: Standard curve
cards.back: A graph built from known values, such as DNA concentrations against absorbance, used to work out an unknown. Also called a calibration curve.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Standard curve

cards.front: Start codon
cards.back: AUG: signals the ribosome to start translation and encodes methionine.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Start codon

cards.front: Sticky ends
cards.back: Short single-stranded overhangs left when a restriction enzyme makes offset cuts, e.g. EcoRI leaves 5′ AATT. They base-pair with ends cut by the same enzyme.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Sticky ends

cards.front: Why do sticky ends make cloning easier?
cards.back: Complementary overhangs base-pair, holding fragments together until DNA ligase seals them.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Sticky ends

cards.front: Stoichiometry
cards.back: The relative quantities of reactants and products in a reaction, shown by the coefficients in a balanced equation. N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃ has a ratio of 1 : 3 → 2.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Stoichiometry

cards.front: What is the stoichiometry of C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O?
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Stoichiometry

cards.front: Stop codon
cards.back: UAA, UAG or UGA: codons that normally encode no amino acid and end translation.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Stop codon

cards.front: Streptococcus pneumoniae
cards.back: The bacterium that is the most common cause of pneumonia. It lives harmlessly in the nose and throat of many healthy people.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Streptococcus pneumoniae

cards.front: Substitution reaction
cards.back: A reaction in which an atom or group on a molecule is replaced by a different one: A + BX → AX + B.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Substitution reaction

cards.front: Give the general form of a substitution.
cards.back: A + BX → AX + B.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Substitution reaction

cards.front: Subunit vaccine approach
cards.back: Vaccines that use just part of the microorganism, such as a protein, sugar or capsid, including inactivated toxins.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Subunit vaccine approach

cards.front: TATA box
cards.back: A eukaryotic promoter sequence bound by the TATA-binding protein to start building the basal transcription complex.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/TATA box

cards.front: TATA-binding protein
cards.back: TBP: binds the TATA box and, with TBP-associated factors (TAFs), brings RNA Pol II to the promoter.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/TATA-binding protein

cards.front: TE buffer
cards.back: Buffer for diluting DNA. Tris keeps the pH stable and EDTA binds the metal ions that DNA-degrading enzymes need.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/TE buffer

cards.front: Taq polymerase
cards.back: A thermostable DNA polymerase from the hot-spring bacterium Thermus aquaticus, the first used for PCR.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Taq polymerase

cards.front: Telomerase
cards.back: The enzyme that adds new repeats to chromosome ends, using its own RNA template, to stop DNA being lost from the ends with each round of replication.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Telomerase

cards.front: Template
cards.back: A strand whose sequence determines the sequence of the new strand copied from it. In replication, each parental strand acts as a template.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Template

cards.front: Template strand
cards.back: The DNA strand RNA polymerase reads. The mRNA is complementary to it.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Template strand

cards.front: Ter sequences
cards.back: 20 bp sequences where replication terminates in E. coli. Bound by the Tus protein, they trap the two forks.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Ter sequences

cards.front: Terminator
cards.back: A sequence that ends transcription. Intrinsic terminators form an RNA hairpin; extrinsic ones need the rho protein.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Terminator

cards.front: Thermocycler
cards.back: The machine that runs PCR by changing the temperature of the samples through each cycle automatically.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Thermocycler

cards.front: Thermodynamic system
cards.back: The part of interest inside a boundary; everything else is the surroundings. Open systems exchange matter and energy, closed systems energy only, isolated systems neither.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Thermodynamic system

cards.front: What does a closed system exchange with its surroundings?
cards.back: Energy but not matter.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Thermodynamic system

cards.front: Thermodynamics
cards.back: The study of energy transformations, energy and heat, and the energy available to do work. First law: energy is conserved. Second law: the entropy of the universe increases.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Thermodynamics

cards.front: Thiol
cards.back: –SH, found in cysteine. Two thiols can form a disulfide bridge.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Thiol

cards.front: Transcription
cards.back: Copying a DNA sequence into RNA. For a protein-coding gene the product is messenger RNA.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Transcription

cards.front: Transcription factor
cards.back: A protein that binds DNA, often at an enhancer, and changes how often transcription starts, up to 100 times more.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Transcription factor

cards.front: Transfer RNA
cards.back: The adaptor RNA that carries an amino acid at its 3′ end and reads a codon with its anticodon. Folds into a cloverleaf.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Transfer RNA

cards.front: What two parts of a tRNA make it an adaptor?
cards.back: The 3′ end, which carries the amino acid, and the anticodon, which pairs with the codon.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Transfer RNA

cards.front: Transformation
cards.back: The uptake of foreign DNA by a cell. Rare in nature, and the basis of both the experiments that identified DNA and modern genetic engineering.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Transformation

cards.front: Transforming principle
cards.back: Griffith's name for whatever passed from dead virulent bacteria to living harmless ones and changed them. Avery, MacLeod and McCarty later showed it was DNA.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Transforming principle

cards.front: Transition state
cards.back: The highest-energy, most unstable arrangement along a reaction step, where bonds are partly broken and partly formed.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Transition state

cards.front: How many transition states does a two-step reaction have?
cards.back: Two.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Transition state

cards.front: Translation
cards.back: Making a protein from an mRNA on ribosomes: the order of codons in the mRNA sets the order of amino acids.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Translation

cards.front: Triplet code
cards.back: The genetic code is read in groups of three bases. Three bases give 4 × 4 × 4 = 64 codons, enough for 20 amino acids; one or two bases would give only 4 or 16.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Triplet code

cards.front: Tus protein
cards.back: The protein that binds Ter sequences and arrests a replication fork approaching from one particular direction.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Tus protein

cards.front: UV absorption
cards.back: DNA and RNA absorb UV light most strongly at 260 nm, because of their bases. It is the standard way to measure nucleic acid concentration and purity.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/UV absorption

cards.front: Universal code
cards.back: Almost all organisms use the same genetic code. Rare exceptions such as selenocysteine and pyrrolysine mean it is not quite universal.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Universal code

cards.front: Untranslated region
cards.back: Parts of an mRNA outside the coding sequence: the 5′ UTR before AUG and the 3′ UTR after the stop codon.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Untranslated region

cards.front: VSEPR theory
cards.back: Valence shell electron pair repulsion: bonds and lone pairs around a central atom spread as far apart as possible, which sets the molecule's shape.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/VSEPR theory

cards.front: Vaccination
cards.back: Deliberate exposure to a preparation from an infectious agent, to induce immunity.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Vaccination

cards.front: Valence shell
cards.back: An atom's outer electron shell. Atoms bond to fill it.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Valence shell

cards.front: Van't Hoff isotherm
cards.back: The link between free energy and the equilibrium constant: ΔrG° = −RT ln K, from ΔrG = ΔrG° + RT ln Q.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Van't Hoff isotherm

cards.front: Virion
cards.back: The extracellular form of a virus. It lets the virus travel between host cells and protects its genome, with surface proteins that help it attach.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Virion

cards.front: Virus
cards.back: An infectious nucleic acid (RNA or DNA) surrounded by protein. It can only replicate inside a host cell, and is not considered alive.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Virus

cards.front: Whole microbe vaccine approach
cards.back: Vaccines that use the whole microbe: live-attenuated (weakened), inactivated (killed), or a recombinant vector.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Whole microbe vaccine approach

cards.front: Wobble hypothesis
cards.back: Crick's proposal that the first two codon bases pair strictly with the tRNA but pairing at the third base is less constrained, so one tRNA can read more than one codon.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Wobble hypothesis

cards.front: X-ray diffraction
cards.back: The technique Rosalind Franklin used. A DNA crystal in an X-ray beam produces a regular pattern of reflections, which revealed the helical structure.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/X-ray diffraction

cards.front: Zoonotic disease
cards.back: An infectious disease of animals that can cause disease when transmitted to humans, such as avian influenza or COVID-19.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Zoonotic disease

cards.front: cAMP
cards.back: Cyclic AMP: made from ATP when glucose is low. It binds CAP to switch on the lac operon, and is a signalling molecule in many cells.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/cAMP

cards.front: dNTP
cards.back: The four DNA building blocks, dATP, dCTP, dGTP and dTTP, that DNA polymerase adds to a growing strand.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/dNTP

cards.front: lacZ
cards.back: The gene for β-galactosidase. In cloning vectors it is a reporter: an insert disrupts it, giving white rather than blue colonies on X-gal.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/lacZ

cards.front: oriC
cards.back: The E. coli origin of replication: 245 bp long, with three repeats of a 13 bp sequence and four repeats of a 9 bp sequence.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/oriC

cards.front: pBR322
cards.back: A circular plasmid used in the practicals. It carries an ampicillin resistance gene (bla), and in Practical 2 its restriction map is worked out.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/pBR322

cards.front: pKa
cards.back: The pH at which an acid is half in its acid form and half in its base form. Buffers work best near their pKa.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/pKa

cards.front: pUC18
cards.back: A widely used E. coli cloning plasmid with an ampicillin resistance gene, the lacZ gene and a polylinker inside lacZ.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/pUC18

cards.front: tsRNA
cards.back: A tRNA-derived small RNA: a fragment cut from a full tRNA molecule, found in sperm, which can carry non-DNA hereditary information to the zygote.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/tsRNA

cards.front: How is BIO-4012Y assessed overall?
cards.back: Exam 50% (25% autumn sitting + 25% summer sitting), Seminar Essay 25%, Clinical Case Study 25%.

cards.back: Seminars 3 to 6 are the four group presentations; seminar 7 is a research laboratory tour.

cards.front: Name the two layers of the airway surface liquid.
cards.back: The periciliary layer (PCL), where the cilia beat, and the mucus layer (M) on top.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Introduction to Biomedicine/Seminars/01 From Bench to Bedside/02 Fluid homeostasis in the conducting airways

cards.front: Which channel absorbs Na⁺ from the airway surface, and what happens to the ASL?
cards.back: ENaC; water follows, so the ASL gets shallower.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Introduction to Biomedicine/Seminars/01 From Bench to Bedside/02 Fluid homeostasis in the conducting airways

cards.front: How does CFTR make the airway surface liquid deeper?
cards.back: It lets Cl⁻ out across the apical membrane; Na⁺ and water follow into the ASL.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Introduction to Biomedicine/Seminars/01 From Bench to Bedside/02 Fluid homeostasis in the conducting airways

cards.front: What is mucociliary clearance?
cards.back: Cilia beating in the periciliary layer move the mucus layer, with what it has trapped, out of the airways.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Introduction to Biomedicine/Seminars/01 From Bench to Bedside/02 Fluid homeostasis in the conducting airways

cards.front: What two things does CFTR need to open?
cards.back: Phosphorylation of its R domain, and ATP binding at NBD1 and NBD2.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Introduction to Biomedicine/Seminars/01 From Bench to Bedside/03 CFTR and how it is activated

cards.front: Which kinases phosphorylate the R domain of CFTR?
cards.back: PKA (activated by cAMP) and PKG-II (activated by cGMP).
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Introduction to Biomedicine/Seminars/01 From Bench to Bedside/03 CFTR and how it is activated

cards.front: Name the domains of CFTR.
cards.back: Two transmembrane domains (TMD1, TMD2), two nucleotide-binding domains (NBD1, NBD2) and a regulatory R domain.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Introduction to Biomedicine/Seminars/01 From Bench to Bedside/03 CFTR and how it is activated

cards.front: What do phosphodiesterases do in CFTR signalling?
cards.back: Break down cAMP and cGMP to AMP and GMP, ending activation.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Introduction to Biomedicine/Seminars/01 From Bench to Bedside/03 CFTR and how it is activated

cards.front: What is the most common CF mutation, and what does it do to the protein?
cards.back: ΔF508 (F508del), deletion of phenylalanine 508; CFTR misfolds in the ER and is degraded, so little reaches the cell surface.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Introduction to Biomedicine/Seminars/01 From Bench to Bedside/04 Cystic fibrosis pathogenesis

cards.front: Why is mucus thick in cystic fibrosis?
cards.back: Too little Cl⁻ (and HCO₃⁻) secretion through CFTR, so too little water enters the airway surface liquid and the mucus dehydrates.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Introduction to Biomedicine/Seminars/01 From Bench to Bedside/04 Cystic fibrosis pathogenesis

cards.front: What is the inheritance pattern of cystic fibrosis?
cards.back: Autosomal recessive.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Introduction to Biomedicine/Seminars/01 From Bench to Bedside/04 Cystic fibrosis pathogenesis

cards.front: Put the drug development stages in order.
cards.back: Drug discovery, pre-clinical, clinical trials (phases I to III), regulatory approval, post-market surveillance.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Introduction to Biomedicine/Seminars/01 From Bench to Bedside/05 The drug discovery pipeline

cards.front: What does ADMET stand for?
cards.back: Absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion and toxicity.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Introduction to Biomedicine/Seminars/01 From Bench to Bedside/05 The drug discovery pipeline

cards.front: Roughly how many compounds enter discovery for each drug approved?
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Introduction to Biomedicine/Seminars/01 From Bench to Bedside/05 The drug discovery pipeline

cards.front: What disease do CFTR ΔF508/ΔF508 pigs show?
cards.back: Gastrointestinal disease at birth, then airway disease that develops spontaneously.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Introduction to Biomedicine/Seminars/01 From Bench to Bedside/06 Modelling cystic fibrosis in vivo, CF pigs

cards.front: Why are pigs used to model CF lung disease?
cards.back: Their lungs and airways are much more like human lungs than those of mice.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Introduction to Biomedicine/Seminars/01 From Bench to Bedside/06 Modelling cystic fibrosis in vivo, CF pigs

cards.front: What is an organoid?
cards.back: A miniature, simplified organ grown in 3D culture from stem cells.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Introduction to Biomedicine/Seminars/01 From Bench to Bedside/07 Organoids as pre-clinical models

cards.front: Which stem cells build intestinal organoids?
cards.back: Lgr5⁺ stem cells from the base of the intestinal crypts.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Introduction to Biomedicine/Seminars/01 From Bench to Bedside/07 Organoids as pre-clinical models

cards.front: Why do wild-type intestinal organoids swell when forskolin is added, and F508del ones do not?
cards.back: Forskolin raises cAMP, opening CFTR; Cl⁻ and water flow into the lumen. F508del organoids have little working CFTR.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Introduction to Biomedicine/Seminars/01 From Bench to Bedside/07 Organoids as pre-clinical models

cards.front: How was it shown that organoid swelling depends on CFTR?
cards.back: Correctors restored swelling in F508del organoids, and a CFTR inhibitor blocked it.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Introduction to Biomedicine/Seminars/01 From Bench to Bedside/07 Organoids as pre-clinical models

cards.front: What kind of defect does the G551D mutation cause?
cards.back: A gating defect: CFTR reaches the cell surface but its ATP-dependent opening does not work.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Introduction to Biomedicine/Seminars/01 From Bench to Bedside/08 Ivacaftor, a bench to bedside case study

cards.front: How does ivacaftor work?
cards.back: It is a potentiator: it binds CFTR at the cell surface and increases the channel's probability of opening.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Introduction to Biomedicine/Seminars/01 From Bench to Bedside/08 Ivacaftor, a bench to bedside case study

cards.front: What is the difference between a CFTR potentiator and a corrector?
cards.back: A potentiator helps a channel already at the surface open; a corrector helps misfolded CFTR fold and reach the surface.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Introduction to Biomedicine/Seminars/01 From Bench to Bedside/08 Ivacaftor, a bench to bedside case study

cards.front: Outline the bench to bedside path for ivacaftor.
cards.back: CFTR gene found (1989) → gating defects understood → high-throughput drug screen → mutation-specific therapy.
cards.note: 01 Year 1/Introduction to Biomedicine/Seminars/01 From Bench to Bedside/08 Ivacaftor, a bench to bedside case study

cards.front: What is Group 4's presentation topic, and when is it?
cards.back: Future therapies for cystic fibrosis (e.g. CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing, gene therapy), in seminar 6.

cards.front: ADMET
cards.back: Absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion and toxicity: drug properties tested in the pre-clinical stage.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/ADMET

cards.front: At which stage is ADMET tested?
cards.back: Pre-clinical.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/ADMET

cards.front: Airway surface liquid
cards.back: The fluid lining the airways: a watery periciliary layer where cilia beat, with a mucus layer on top. Its depth is set by ion transport through CFTR and ENaC.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Airway surface liquid

cards.front: What sets the depth of the airway surface liquid?
cards.back: The balance of Cl⁻ secretion (CFTR) and Na⁺ absorption (ENaC), which water follows.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Airway surface liquid

cards.front: CFTR
cards.back: An ATP-gated anion channel (an ABC protein) in the apical membrane of epithelial cells that secretes Cl⁻ and HCO₃⁻. Opens when its R domain is phosphorylated and ATP binds NBD1 and NBD2.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/CFTR

cards.front: What must happen for CFTR to open?
cards.back: R domain phosphorylation (by PKA or PKG-II) and ATP binding at NBD1 and NBD2.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/CFTR

cards.front: CFTR corrector
cards.back: A drug that helps misfolded CFTR, such as F508del, fold and traffic to the cell surface, e.g. VRT-325 and Corr-4a.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/CFTR corrector

cards.front: What do correctors do?
cards.back: Help misfolded CFTR fold and reach the cell surface.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/CFTR corrector

cards.front: CFTR potentiator
cards.back: A drug that increases the opening of CFTR channels already at the cell surface, e.g. ivacaftor.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/CFTR potentiator

cards.front: Which mutation class do potentiators treat?
cards.back: Gating defects, such as G551D.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/CFTR potentiator

cards.front: Cystic fibrosis
cards.back: An autosomal recessive disease caused by mutations in the CFTR gene. Too little Cl⁻ secretion leaves thick, dehydrated mucus, especially in the lungs and gut.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Cystic fibrosis

cards.front: What gene is mutated in cystic fibrosis?
cards.back: CFTR.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Cystic fibrosis

cards.front: ENaC
cards.back: The apical epithelial Na⁺ channel that absorbs Na⁺ from the airway surface, so water follows and the airway surface liquid gets shallower.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/ENaC

cards.front: What does ENaC do to the airway surface liquid?
cards.back: Absorbs Na⁺, so water follows and the ASL gets shallower.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/ENaC

cards.front: F508del
cards.back: The most common CF mutation: deletion of phenylalanine 508 of CFTR. The protein misfolds in the ER and is degraded, so little reaches the cell surface.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/F508del

cards.front: Where does F508del CFTR get stuck?
cards.back: In the endoplasmic reticulum, where it is degraded.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/F508del

cards.front: Forskolin-induced swelling
cards.back: An organoid test of CFTR function: forskolin raises cAMP and opens CFTR, so organoids with working CFTR swell with fluid.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Forskolin-induced swelling

cards.front: What does lack of swelling in the forskolin assay show?
cards.back: Little functional CFTR, as in F508del organoids.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Forskolin-induced swelling

cards.front: G551D
cards.back: A CFTR missense mutation (glycine to aspartic acid at 551) that causes a gating defect: the channel reaches the surface but does not open properly.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/G551D

cards.front: Which drug targets G551D CFTR?
cards.back: Ivacaftor, a potentiator.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/G551D

cards.front: Ivacaftor
cards.back: A CFTR potentiator that increases the opening probability of gating-defective CFTR such as G551D. The first licensed drug to target the underlying defect in CF.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Ivacaftor

cards.front: What type of CFTR modulator is ivacaftor?
cards.back: A potentiator.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Ivacaftor

cards.front: Lgr5
cards.back: A marker of intestinal stem cells at the base of the crypts. A single Lgr5⁺ cell can grow into an intestinal organoid.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Lgr5

cards.front: What can a single Lgr5⁺ stem cell build in culture?
cards.back: An intestinal organoid with crypt-villus structures.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Lgr5

cards.front: Mucociliary clearance
cards.back: Removal of mucus, and the particles and bacteria trapped in it, from the airways by beating cilia.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Mucociliary clearance

cards.front: Why does mucociliary clearance fail in CF?
cards.back: The airway surface liquid is too shallow and the mucus too thick for the cilia to move it.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Mucociliary clearance

cards.front: Organoid
cards.back: A miniature, simplified organ grown in 3D culture from stem cells, with realistic microanatomy.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Organoid

cards.front: Why are patient-derived organoids useful for CF?
cards.back: They carry the patient's own CFTR mutations, so drugs can be tested on them.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Organoid

cards.front: Precision medicine
cards.back: Treatment targeted to an individual's specific molecular defect or genotype, e.g. ivacaftor for G551D CF.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Precision medicine

cards.front: Why is ivacaftor called a landmark in precision medicine?
cards.back: It targets a specific molecular defect, the gating defect of mutations such as G551D.
cards.note: 02 Key Terms/Precision medicine
